Driftwood business stuff. There's a Christmas craft fair at the Galway Arts Centre in early December and the application asks a bunch of questions. I've drafted answers but they're all a bit "I like wood". Help me make them sound like a real business without sounding like a wanker:

"1. Tell us about your business (max 150 words).
Driftwood Restoration is a one-man furniture restoration business based in Galway. I restore old furniture, mainly Irish pieces from the 1900s to the 1970s, and also make some new pieces like benches and small tables. I've been doing this for about six years as a side business alongside my teaching job.

2. What will you be selling at the fair?
I will be selling some small restored pieces like stools, a blanket box and a few chairs. I will also have some new small items like chopping boards and coasters made from offcuts. And I'll have information about the restoration service.

3. What makes your work unique?
I try to keep as much of the original piece as possible. I use traditional methods like hide glue and French polish. I like to find out the history of the piece if I can.

4. Price range of items.
Coasters 8 euro for 4, chopping boards 25-45 euro, stools 80-150 euro, chairs 120-200 euro, blanket box 350 euro.

5. Do you have any sustainability practices?
I reuse old wood. The offcuts become chopping boards. Restoring furniture is better than buying new.

6. Space requirements.
One standard stall (2m x 1m table). No electricity needed.

7. Social media / website.
Instagram @driftwood.restoration.galway. No website yet."

That's so much better. The opening line "Every piece of old furniture has outlived someone who loved it. My job is to make sure it outlives the next person too." — that's a bit grand but I actually like it. It's true.
And in sustainability, adding the actual number, I estimated I've kept around 120 pieces out of landfill over 6 years, that's more convincing than "better than buying new".

The craft fair is on the 5th and 6th of December. The 6th is a Sunday. So I'd do Saturday only, if they allow that, or get one of my brothers to mind the stall on the Sunday. Is it normal to ask for one day only?

Height at the back with the stools, chopping boards fanned in the middle, coasters at the front for the impulse buy, and a framed "before and after" photo of the Kelly sideboard when it's done. Love it. If Maeve ever sends me the fabric, the chairs could be in there too.

Ok, unrelated, my mother's Christmas cake recipe. I found her handwritten card in a drawer and I want to make it this year, first time since she passed. Some of it's hard to read and some of it is in "Mam measurements". Can you help me convert it?

"Mam's Christmas Cake
1 lb sultanas, 1 lb raisins, half lb currants, 4 oz cherries (wash them!!), 2 oz mixed peel
Soak all the fruit in a good glass of whiskey (not the good whiskey) overnight, or a few nights if you remember
half lb butter, half lb brown sugar, cream them till your arm is sore
5 eggs, one at a time, a spoon of the flour with each so it doesn't curdle
10 oz plain flour, 1 tsp mixed spice, half tsp cinnamon, a good grating of nutmeg, pinch of salt
2 oz ground almonds
grated rind of a lemon and an orange
Mix the fruit in last with a big spoon not the mixer
Line a 9 inch tin with two layers of brown paper and tie newspaper round the outside
Low oven (gas 2) for about 4 hours, test with a skewer, don't open the door for the first 2 hours or it'll sink and it'll be your own fault
Feed it with whiskey every week until Christmas (the cake not your father)"
Ha, "the cake not your father". That's her exactly. Ok so in grams and a fan oven temperature. Gas 2 is about 150C, so 130C fan. Got it.
Can I make it without the ground almonds? Cian's friend Rory has a nut allergy and he's here a lot over Christmas.

Grand, swap the ground almonds for the same weight of extra flour or a bit of breadcrumbs, and check the mixed peel and cherries for "may contain nuts" labels. Good shout. I'll make it nut-free and keep it safe.
When should I make it? It's October now.
End of October or early November gives it time to be fed. I'll do it the weekend after next. Not Sunday. Obviously. Saturday baking with the kids, Mam would like that.
Thanks. Right, Vanessa needs diesel and Cian needs a lift to training. Night.

A past student, Aoibheann, emailed asking me to write a reference for her application to study history and archaeology in Edinburgh. She was in my Leaving Cert class two years ago, took a gap year. She sent me her personal statement so I know what she's saying about herself. Can you read it and help me write a reference that complements it rather than repeating it?

"Ever since I found a clay pipe stem in my grandmother's garden in Clifden when I was nine, I have wanted to understand how ordinary people lived in the past. That small piece of white clay, probably dropped by a farm labourer in the nineteenth century, made me realise that history is not only about kings and battles but about people whose names were never written down.

At school, history was my favourite subject. I was particularly drawn to the social history of nineteenth-century Ireland, and for my Leaving Certificate research study I investigated the impact of the Famine on the Clifden workhouse, using the Board of Guardians minute books held in the county archives. Reading the handwritten records of admissions and deaths was an emotional experience, and it taught me how much can be learned from sources that were never intended for historians. My research study received an A grade.

During my gap year I volunteered for four months with a community archaeology project in Connemara, excavating a deserted pre-Famine village. I learned basic excavation techniques, how to record contexts and finds, and how to work as part of a team in difficult conditions, often in the rain. I was surprised by how much of archaeology is careful recording rather than discovery, but I found that I enjoyed the patience it requires. I also gave tours of the site to visiting school groups, which helped me develop confidence in explaining complex ideas simply.

I have also worked part-time in a café in Galway, which has taught me time management and how to deal with people, including difficult ones. In my free time I read widely, particularly social history and historical fiction, and I play the fiddle in a traditional music session every Thursday.

I am applying to study History and Archaeology because I want to combine the documentary evidence I enjoyed working with in school with the material evidence I discovered in the field. I am particularly interested in the archaeology of rural communities and how material culture can give a voice to people who left few written records. I hope to eventually work in heritage or research, perhaps focusing on the archaeology of the Irish diaspora.

Edinburgh's combination of strong historical and archaeological departments, and its fieldwork opportunities, make it the ideal place for me to pursue these interests."

Lovely statement. She was genuinely one of the best students I've had. Here's what I can add that she can't say about herself: she was the one who organised the class trip to the county archives for everyone else; she helped a struggling classmate with his research study without being asked; her research study was among the best I've marked in 16 years; and she argued with me, politely and with evidence, about the role of the Catholic Church in the Famine relief, and she was partly right.
That's great. Keep the bit about her arguing with me, universities love independent thinkers. Can you make it about 350 words, formal but warm? UK universities like a structured reference apparently.

Perfect. I'll sign it as "Mr. Liam O'Driscoll, Teacher of History and Geography, St. Enda's Community School". Should I mention I'm her former teacher only, or that I'm also the trip leader etc.? Doesn't matter really.
Grand, just subject teacher. Thanks.
Unrelated: the kids want to carve pumpkins for Halloween. Do they still do turnips in Ireland or is it all American pumpkins now? I want to tell them the history.

Right, turnips were the original Irish jack-o'-lanterns, terrifying things, and the pumpkin came back from America. I'll make them carve one turnip each as a history lesson, then they can have pumpkins. They'll hate me for about ten minutes.
And Samhain, the actual origin. Short version please, for a 9 and 13 year old.

Good. The thin veil between the living and the dead, bonfires, disguises so spirits wouldn't recognise you. Cian will want to dress up as a spirit. Saoirse will roll her eyes and then secretly dress up anyway.
Thanks. Night.

For my history society talk on 1920s Galway, I found an old newspaper report in the archives. It's dense and old-fashioned. Can you help me pull out the interesting human details I could use? Here's the transcription:

"GALWAY NOTES. The past week has been one of considerable activity in the city, notwithstanding the continued inclemency of the weather. The new picture house in Middle Street, which opened its doors to the public on Saturday evening last, was thronged to capacity, and it is reported that many persons were obliged to be turned away at the door. The programme consisted of an American drama of the West, together with a comic subject which provoked much laughter, and an orchestra of four performers provided musical accompaniment. The management announces that there will be a special matinee on Wednesday for the children of the city schools, at a reduced price of twopence. It is to be hoped that this new form of amusement will not draw the young people away from more improving pursuits.

At the Claddagh, the fishermen report poor catches for the season, the herring having failed to appear in their usual numbers. Several families are said to be in some distress, and the St. Vincent de Paul Society has made arrangements for the distribution of coal and provisions. A meeting of the fishermen was held on Thursday at which it was resolved to petition the Minister for Fisheries for assistance in the purchase of new nets and the repair of boats damaged in the storms of the previous month.

The County Council met on Tuesday, when the question of the Irish language in the schools of the county again occupied the members for a considerable time. Mr. Ó Flaithearta proposed that the Council should request the Department to ensure that teachers appointed to schools in the Irish-speaking districts be competent in the language, a proposal which was carried after a lengthy debate. Some members expressed concern that the requirement might cause difficulty in obtaining teachers.

On Sunday the annual excursion of the Galway Workmen's Club to Salthill took place, favoured, for once, by fine weather. Upwards of three hundred members and their families travelled by brake and on foot to the promenade, where sports were held for the children and a band played selections. The bathing was not largely availed of, the water being described by those who ventured in as 'very fresh'.

The price of eggs at Saturday's market was 1s 4d per dozen, butter 1s 8d per lb, and potatoes 6d per stone. Turf was plentiful."

Brilliant. The new cinema crowd turned away at the door, the hope that it "will not draw young people away from more improving pursuits" (ha, the 1920s version of worrying about phones), the herring failing in the Claddagh, the Irish teachers debate (which is still going on, basically), and people bathing at Salthill in "very fresh" water. Dad would've been one of them in a later decade.
Can you help me turn the prices into something modern people would understand? Like, what's 1s 4d for a dozen eggs relative to wages then?
Right, a labourer earning maybe 30-40 shillings a week, so eggs were a real cost. That's a nice way to show it, "a dozen eggs was about an hour's wages". Ok.
I'll use the "very fresh" line as my closing joke. A Galway audience will appreciate that nothing has changed in 100 years.
Different question: is "brake" in that article a type of carriage? I assume it's not a car brake.
Right, a large horse-drawn wagon for groups. Good, I'll explain that. Thanks, that was fun. Proper history nerd evening.
Night.

"BUSINESS PLAN - 'ReLove Furniture' (TY Mini Company, St. Enda's)
Team: Ciara (Managing Director), Oisín (Finance), Méabh (Marketing), Tadhg (Production)

1. Our idea: We will collect old furniture that people don't want, like chairs, small tables and stools, and upcycle them by sanding, painting them in bright colours and adding new handles or fabric. Then we will sell them at school events, at the Christmas craft fair and on Instagram. Our slogan is 'Old furniture, new love'.

2. Our market: Students' parents, teachers, young people moving into their first apartment, and people who care about the environment. Galway has a lot of students and young people who can't afford new furniture and like unique things.

3. Our competitors: IKEA (but our stuff is unique and more sustainable), charity shops (but our stuff is upcycled and nicer), and other upcycling people on Instagram (but we are students, so people will want to support us).

4. Getting furniture: We will ask our families, neighbours and teachers for unwanted furniture. We will also check the free section on DoneDeal and Facebook Marketplace.

5. Costs: Paint - 15 euro per tin, we think 6 tins = 90 euro. Sandpaper - 20 euro. Brushes - 25 euro. New handles - 2 euro each, maybe 30 handles = 60 euro. Fabric - 40 euro. Instagram ads - 30 euro. Transport - we will ask our parents. Total: 265 euro.

6. Prices: Chairs 35 euro, stools 25 euro, small tables 50 euro, bigger pieces 80+ euro.

7. Sales target: We want to sell 20 pieces by Easter, which would make about 800 euro.

8. Profit: 800 - 265 = 535 euro profit, which we will split between us and give 10% to Galway Simon Community.

9. Risks: We might not get enough furniture. Painting might take longer than we think. People might not buy. Someone might get hurt using tools.

10. Production: We will work in the school woodwork room on Wednesday afternoons with permission from Mr. Burke."

Agreed, it's a good start. Main gaps: they haven't counted their own time, transport is a big hidden cost ("ask our parents" is not a plan), they need a sanding/finishing safety plan with Mr. Burke, and the sales target might be optimistic given they can only work on Wednesdays. And their competitor section is a bit "we're nicer".
I like the idea of them doing a "test batch" of 3 pieces first, time how long each takes, and set prices from that. Real data, not guesses. Gráinne would approve, ha.
Can you write feedback in a format I can give them as a group, with 3 "what's great" and 3 "what to work on"? Keep the language encouraging.
Perfect. Also, should I let them use my van for collecting furniture? Probably not, insurance-wise?
Yeah, no, I'm not insured to transport students' business stock, and the school would have a fit. Parents with cars, with a sign-off form. Fine.

Different thing. I'm taking the kids to Dublin for a weekend in half-term, staying with my brother Ger, and I want to do one history thing with them that won't bore them. I'm thinking Kilmainham Gaol. Here's the info from the website, is it suitable for a 9 year old?

"Kilmainham Gaol - Visitor Information
Kilmainham Gaol is one of the largest unoccupied gaols in Europe. Built in 1796, it held many of the leaders of Irish rebellions, from the 1798 United Irishmen to the leaders of the 1916 Rising, fourteen of whom were executed in the Stonebreakers' Yard in May 1916. The gaol also held ordinary men, women and children, many imprisoned for petty crimes such as stealing food during the Great Famine. Some prisoners were as young as seven years old.
Access to the gaol is by guided tour only, lasting approximately one hour, followed by self-guided access to the museum exhibition. The tour includes the chapel, the old West Wing with its narrow cells, the Victorian East Wing (featured in many films), and the Stonebreakers' Yard where the 1916 executions took place.
Tours are suitable for all ages; however, some content deals with themes of imprisonment, hardship and execution, which parents may wish to discuss with younger children beforehand. Parts of the gaol are cold and dimly lit, and visitors are advised to wear warm clothing.
Tickets must be booked online in advance and tours frequently sell out, particularly at weekends and during school holidays. Admission: Adult EUR 8, Child EUR 4, Family ticket (2 adults and up to 3 children) EUR 20. Under-12s must be accompanied by an adult.
Getting here: Kilmainham Gaol is located approximately 3.5 km west of Dublin city centre. Luas Red Line to Suir Road (10-minute walk) or Dublin Bus routes 13, 40 and 69."

Grand, so suitable but I'll prep Cian beforehand, especially the bit about children being imprisoned for stealing food. That'll actually land with him, he's a big believer in fairness. And book online, holidays sell out.
Saoirse will want to see the East Wing because it's in some film she's seen. Fine, a hook's a hook.
And something fun after so it doesn't end on executions. Ideas nearby?
The Phoenix Park and the zoo, perfect, it's a bus ride away. History in the morning, giraffes in the afternoon, chips on the way home. That's a well-balanced day.
Should I book the Saturday or Sunday? Ger's working Saturday morning.
Saturday it is, just me and the kids, and Ger can meet us at the zoo after. And Sunday we're doing nothing but lying on Ger's couch. Thanks, sorted.
Night.

Quick one before bed. Saoirse asked me why Galway is called "the City of the Tribes" and I gave her the short version, but she wants the proper story for a school project. Can you give me the key points?

Right, the fourteen merchant families who dominated the town's trade and politics from the medieval period, the Lynches, Blakes, Frenchs and the rest, and Cromwell's forces using "tribes" as an insult that the families then adopted with pride. That's a nice twist for a 13 year old: taking an insult and making it a badge.
And the Lynch Memorial Window story, the mayor who supposedly hanged his own son? Is that true or a legend?

Grand, so it's a legend with very shaky evidence, and the word "lynching" almost certainly doesn't come from it, whatever the tour guides say. Good. I'll tell her to present it as a legend and say why historians doubt it. That's proper history.

sessions: Hello, nice to meet you. My name is Yuki Tanabe. I am a freelance translator, Japanese to English mostly, sometimes English to Japanese. I live in Osaka, in Kita-ku, near Tenma, with my cat Mochi. My English is good for work but in casual writing sometimes strange, please forgive me.

First, a small question for warming up. How would you translate 「もったいない」 in a literary text? Not a business text. Every dictionary says "wasteful" but it feels too cold. The context is an old woman looking at a half-eaten persimmon her grandson left on the table.

Ah, I like your idea that sometimes we should not translate the word itself but the feeling around it. "She couldn't bear to see it go to waste" or even showing her picking it up and finishing it herself. The action can carry the word. Yes.

Some information about me, maybe useful later. I work best in the morning, from about 6 until lunch. Please never suggest calls or meetings after 9pm Japan time, I am finished by then, my brain becomes tofu. Many of my clients are in Europe so this is always a negotiation.
Also I have an allergy to buckwheat, quite serious. So no soba, and careful with some galettes and some Japanese sweets. If you suggest recipes or restaurants, please remember.

Now big news for me. A London publisher, Harbor Lane Press, offered me to translate a novel. It is 『塩の果樹園』 by Kawabe Rin, in English "The Salt Orchard". It is a quiet novel about a family running a mikan orchard in Wakayama near the sea, three generations, and the youngest daughter comes back from Tokyo. I love this book. It is my first full literary novel. Until now I did short stories and a lot of commercial work.
The editor at Harbor Lane is Thomas Pryce. He found me through a short story translation I did for a literary magazine. He is very kind, writes long emails with many semicolons.

The contract is not finished yet. They sent the terms and I agreed, but their legal team must prepare it and countersign. Until the contract is signed I don't want to start properly. Is that too careful?
Yes, I think so too. I will do some light reading and glossary preparation but not the real translation until it is signed. Thank you.
Can I ask about rates? For literary translation into English in the UK, what is a normal rate? They offered per 1,000 words. I want to know if it is fair before I sign.
Okay, so the Society of Authors gives guidance and what they offered is in the normal range, not high but fair for a first novel. Good, I feel better.
Last small thing: my cat Mochi has started to sleep on my keyboard every morning at exactly 6:30. Is there a scientific reason? She is ruining my best working hour.
Ha, warmth and attention. I will put a heated pad next to the laptop. Mochi, you win again. Thank you, see you next time.

Hello again. Today family topic. My younger sister Aoi is getting married! I am so happy. Her fiancé is Daniel Weber, he is German, works as an engineer in Kobe. They met at a climbing gym. He is very tall and very polite and he is learning Japanese very hard.

The wedding will be in Kyoto, at Kamogawa Garden Hall, near the river. The date is 11 April next year. Aoi asked me to give a speech at the reception, in Japanese and English both, because Daniel's family is coming from Hamburg.

I am nervous. I translate other people's words all day but my own words in front of 80 people, that is different. Can you give me some advice about structure of a bilingual wedding speech? Should I say everything twice?

Ah, I see, not everything twice, it becomes too long. Better to alternate: one part in Japanese, the next part in English, with small summary. And the most important line maybe in both. That is clever.
What are typical things not to say in a Japanese wedding speech? I know there are 忌み言葉 like "cut" or "separate" or "return". Can you list more so I can avoid them in both languages?
Oh, I forgot about repeated words like 「重ね重ね」 or 「たびたび」, because they suggest remarriage. In English I don't need to worry, but in the Japanese part, yes. Thank you.

Also Aoi wants me to help her choose a kimono for the 前撮り photo, the photo before the wedding. She is choosing between a white shiromuku and a colourful iro-uchikake. I don't have opinion, I just want her happy. What is the difference in meaning?
Interesting, the white means she is ready to be "dyed" in the colour of the new family, and the colourful one was for after the ceremony traditionally. Daniel will like this story. I will tell him.

And one more: Daniel asked me how to say "thank you for raising such a wonderful daughter" to my parents in Japanese, in a natural way, not like a textbook. Can you help? He wants to say it at the reception.
「素敵な娘さんを育ててくださって、本当にありがとうございます」 is good. Maybe I will teach him to bow a little at the end. He will practise in front of the mirror, he is that type.
Thank you! I feel a little more ready.

Hello. Today work. Harbor Lane still did not send the countersigned contract, but Thomas said to send him a sample of the first pages anyway so he can see my voice. Not official translation, just a sample. I think this is ok.

Here is my draft of the opening paragraphs. Please do not rewrite, but tell me where the rhythm feels "translated" and not natural English:

"The sea was visible from every row of the orchard, though no one in the Mizuno family ever looked at it. It was simply there, the way the sky was there, the way Grandmother's cough was there in the mornings, a fact of the place rather than a view. The trees grew in terraces up the hillside, each terrace held by a stone wall that had been built by hands no one living could name, and in winter the mikan hung among the dark leaves like small lamps someone had forgotten to put out.

Haruka came back in the second week of December, when the harvest was half finished and everyone was too tired to ask her why. She arrived on the last bus from Gobo, carrying one suitcase and a paper bag of Tokyo sweets that nobody would eat, because they were too sweet and too small and because they were from Tokyo. Her father met her at the bus stop with the light truck. He did not get out. He leaned across and opened the passenger door from inside, and the smell of the truck, oil and fruit and his cigarettes, which he had promised to stop, reached her before his voice did.

'You're thin,' he said.

'You're still smoking,' she said.

They drove up the hill without speaking further. Below them, the sea did what it always did, and neither of them looked at it."

Thank you. So, mostly it flows, but "a fact of the place rather than a view" maybe a little too clever, and "small lamps someone had forgotten to put out" is good but "forgotten" maybe should be "forgotten to turn off"? Hmm, no, "put out" is better for old lamps with flame. I keep it.

And you think "because they were from Tokyo" at the end of the list is good because the original also has this little joke? Yes, the original is 「東京のものだったから」, it is a small bitter joke. I am glad it survives.

Thomas also asked about the schedule. I told him I can deliver the first half, chapters 1 to 12, by 5 November, and the full draft at the end of January. He said that works for their plan to publish in spring 2028.
Spring 2028 seems so far! Is it normal that publishing is so slow? Two years after translation?
I see, editing, copyediting, proofs, cover design, sales catalogue, they need the book a year before for the sales team. Okay, it makes sense. Patience is part of the job.
Small question about style: should I keep Japanese honorifics like "-san" and "Obaachan" in the English, or translate them to "Grandma" and "Mr."? Thomas did not say yet.

I like your answer: decide one rule and be consistent, and for family words like Obaachan maybe translate to "Grandmother" because it is about the relationship, but keep names. I will propose this to Thomas.
Okay, I go back to work. Mochi is on the keyboard again, heated pad failed.
Hello. Today not work, life admin.

My landlord, Mr. Okada, sent a letter: rent goes up from next year, from 78,000 yen to 85,000. He is a nice old man, he apologised two times in the letter. The apartment is small, 1LDK, and I work from the living room, which is also bedroom when I fold my futon. I am thinking maybe it is time to move.

I am looking at Suita, near Esaka station. Cheaper than Tenma for more space, and I could have a 2LDK with one room only for work. But I like Tenma, the shopping street, my favourite izakaya, the old man at the tofu shop who knows Mochi's name. I don't know. Nothing decided.
Can you help me make a comparison? Commute doesn't matter so much because I work from home, but I go to Umeda maybe two times a week for meetings or co-working.
That is helpful. Esaka is only 10 minutes to Umeda on the Midosuji line. And more space for the same money. Hmm. But the tofu man. I will think more.
Different topic: tax. As a freelancer I do 確定申告 every year with blue form, 青色申告. This year I will receive money from a UK publisher. How does tax work for foreign income? Will the UK take tax first?

Ah, the UK-Japan tax treaty, and I should send a form so the UK publisher doesn't withhold tax, and then I declare it in Japan normally. I will ask Harbor Lane for this form when the contract comes. Thank you, I didn't know.
Also, my accountant friend says I should start "invoicing in yen" for foreign clients. Is that common? Or better in their currency?
I see, depends on who takes the exchange risk. For UK publisher, pounds is normal. Okay, I will not be difficult.

Unrelated, but I am curious: why do British people say "cheers" for thank you and for goodbye and for drinking? Thomas writes "cheers" at the end of every email and once wrote "cheers for the cheers" and I didn't understand.
Ha, "thanks for saying thanks". British humour, very dry. I like him more now.
Thank you, good night.

Hello! The Harbor Lane contract arrived, finally. I signed it today and sent it back. Now waiting for their side to countersign. I will upload it so you have the details. It is long so I copied the main parts as text.
Can you check if anything is strange? Especially the deadlines and the payment. I have never had a literary contract before.
Okay, so: fee per 1,000 words, paid in thirds, the deadlines, the credit on the cover, royalty after advance earns out. Nothing strange, you say it is a fair standard contract. I'm relieved.

The part about "house style: British English spelling" — I learned American spelling at school and in most of my commercial work. I need to be careful: colour, realise, travelling. Do you know a good way to set Word to British English for one document only?
Thank you. Done. The red lines everywhere now under my "color". It feels like being corrected by a strict teacher.
Also it says I will be credited on the cover. Thomas said in an email this is Harbor Lane's policy for all translations. I'm so happy about that. My name on the cover of a real book.
What is "moral right to be identified"? It's in clause 9.
Okay, so even if they change something, my name must be connected to my work, and I can object to bad treatment. Good.
I will start translating properly when they countersign. Thomas says "a few days". Fingers crossed.

Good news! Harbor Lane countersigned the contract. Thomas sent the PDF this morning with a very British email: "Delighted to say we're all signed and sealed; welcome aboard properly." So now the Kawabe book is officially my job. I started chapter 1 today at 6am, with coffee and Mochi on my feet instead of the keyboard (heated pad finally works).

But now I have a new worry. The novel uses a lot of Kishu dialect, 紀州弁, in the dialogue of the grandmother and the father. Some expressions I can guess, but some I really don't know if they are dialect or the author's own invention. The contract says questions to the author go through her agent, Ms. Fujimori at Tsubaki Literary Agency. I prepared a list of questions. Can you check my English is polite and clear? She reads English but I will also write in Japanese.

"Dear Ms. Fujimori,
Thank you for your support with the English translation of Shio no Kajuen. I have begun the translation and I would be very grateful if you could pass the following questions to Kawabe-sensei. I understand she is busy, so there is no rush, but answers before the end of October would help me very much to finish the first half on schedule.

1. Chapter 2, p. 31: The grandmother says 「ほんまにあんたはいっつもよう言わんわ」. I understand 'よう言わん' as 'I can't say it / I don't have the heart to say it', but in context it might be an expression of exasperated affection. Which is closer to the intended nuance?
2. Chapter 3, p. 48: The word 「あがら」 appears in the father's speech. I believe this is Kishu dialect for 'we/us'. Is it used here to emphasise the family as a group against outsiders, or is it simply his normal speech?
3. Chapter 4, p. 66: 「つれ」 — in Kishu dialect I believe this can mean 'friend' rather than 'companion/spouse'. Could you confirm?
4. Chapter 5, p. 79: The phrase 「みかんの木は塩を覚えとる」 ('the mikan trees remember the salt') — is this a local saying, or the author's own image? If it is a local saying, I would like to add a short note for English readers.
5. Chapter 7, p. 112: Haruka's mother uses standard Japanese while everyone else uses dialect. Is this intentional, to show she is from outside the region? I want to reflect this difference in the English.
6. General: Would Kawabe-sensei prefer that the dialect be rendered with a regional English flavour, or in neutral English with occasional rhythm differences? I have prepared a short sample of both approaches if she would like to see them.

With many thanks and best regards,
Yuki Tanabe"
Thank you, only small changes, good. I like your suggestion to attach the sample of both approaches directly instead of offering. Less back and forth.
For the sample, how would you render the grandmother's dialect in English without making her sound like a stereotype? I am afraid of making her sound like a cowboy or a pirate.

Yes, exactly, I don't want her to be Irish or Scottish by accident. Your idea: keep grammar mostly standard but use rhythm, shortened forms, a few old-fashioned words, and repetition. Like an old woman from the countryside anywhere. That feels right.
Okay, I sent it to Ms. Fujimori. Now I wait. Translators always wait.
Small Japanese question, because I'm tired and my brain is mixing: in English, "persimmon" — British people know this fruit? Or should I say "sharon fruit"?
Okay, "persimmon" is known enough, and "sharon fruit" is a specific variety marketing name. Persimmon it is.
Thank you. Good night, Mochi says goodnight too (she doesn't, she is asleep).
Hello! Another job came. This time a video game. I love games so I'm excited.

The company is Pinecone Games, a small indie studio in Stockholm. The game is called "Lantern Keeper", it's a cozy puzzle adventure about a girl who keeps the lighthouse lanterns lit on a group of islands. It was originally written in Japanese by the director, who is Japanese and lives in Sweden, and they need English localisation. The producer is Elin Berg. She is very organised, she sent me a spreadsheet with colour codes before we even talked about price.
The game release is planned for 26 February 2027 on Steam and Switch. So that's a different timeline from the book. Two big projects at the same time, scary but exciting.

The problem: they sent me the text strings in a spreadsheet but no access to the game build, no screenshots, no character sheet. I don't know who is speaking to whom, if the girl is talking to her grandfather or to a cat (there is a talking cat). In Japanese, speech style tells me a lot, but I need to see the context. Without it I can't really start.
How do I ask for the build politely but firmly? Game companies sometimes worry about leaks.
Good, I will mention I can sign an NDA, and that without context the quality will suffer and they will pay for more revision rounds later. Business argument, not emotional argument.
Can you explain the difference between localisation and translation? Elin used "localisation" every time and I want to sound professional when I talk to her.
Yes, localisation includes cultural adaptation, UI length limits, jokes, names, even changing references. In this game there is a joke about 「おでん」 that won't work in English. I will think about it.

Also another offer came yesterday, from a manga publisher in the US, Kitsune Comics. They want me to translate a slice-of-life manga series, 8 volumes. The pay is lower than literary but steady. I don't know if I can take it with the novel and the game. Maybe yes from next year? I haven't answered. I really don't know.

Can you help me think about capacity? Novel: about 92,000 words by end of January. Game: maybe 50,000 words, deadline in December. I translate about 2,500 to 3,000 polished words per day on literary, more on game text.
Hmm, so with both, I'm almost full until January, and manga would make me too busy. But maybe I can start manga in February. I will tell Kitsune I need time to think. Thank you.
Last question: what is "cozy game"? Elin keeps saying "cozy" with z. Is it American spelling?
Ah, "cosy" is British and "cozy" is American. Funny, the book is British spelling and the game is maybe American. I need to ask Elin which English they want.
Thank you, bye!

Hello. Some sad news, work-related. Thomas Pryce is leaving Harbor Lane! He got a job as editorial director at a bigger publisher. He told me personally by email, it was very kind. He said the book is in very good hands.

My new editor is Grace Odum. She has been at Harbor Lane for six years, she edited their Korean and Indonesian translations, so she knows translated fiction. Thomas introduced us by email yesterday and from now on I work with her. Thomas's last day is this Friday.

I'm a bit sad because Thomas found me and believed in me. But Grace's first email was very warm. She said she had read my sample and "the bus stop scene made me cry on the Tube". That's a good beginning.
Can you help me write a thank you email to Thomas? I want to say goodbye properly. Not too emotional, he is British.
Perfect. "Cheers for everything, including the cheers" — he will laugh. Thank you.
And a first email to Grace, introducing myself and my plan for the first half, and asking if she has any preferences for how I send queries? Not too long.
Good. Also I want to mention the honorifics decision I proposed to Thomas: names keep, family words become English. Thomas agreed, but I should confirm with Grace, new editor, new opinions maybe.
Sent. She replied within one hour: she agrees with the honorifics rule and she prefers queries as comments in the Word document. Very efficient.

Unrelated: I'm reading a book on translation theory, Lawrence Venuti, "The Translator's Invisibility". He talks about "domestication" and "foreignization". Can you explain simply? The book is very dense.

Okay, domestication = make it feel like it was written in English, smooth; foreignization = keep some strangeness so the reader feels it's from another culture. And Venuti says English translations domesticate too much and make translators invisible. Interesting, and a little political.
Where would you put my opening paragraphs? I think somewhere in the middle. I kept "mikan" not "tangerine".
Yes, I agree. A little foreignization with mikan, but the sentences are natural English. Okay. Thank you, my brain is full now.

Hello. I need to correct something I said before, sorry. The first half delivery for the novel is 15 November, not the 5th. I looked at the signed contract again and it says 15 November clearly. I told you and Thomas "5 November" from my memory. Grace also confirmed: 15 November for chapters 1 to 12.
Ten more days, I'm so relieved. That gives me time if Ms. Fujimori is slow with the answers.
Progress: I have finished chapters 1 to 4 in first draft. About 28,000 Japanese characters translated into maybe 26,000 English words. Hmm, is that right? I always confuse the conversion.

Ah, roughly, Japanese characters to English words, often around 0.5 to 0.7 English words per character depending on the text? So maybe it's less, 14,000 to 18,000 words. Let me check with Word count. ... 16,400 words. Okay, your estimate was right, my first number was crazy.

Can I ask about something difficult in chapter 4? There is a scene where the father says 「お前はもう、ここの人間とちゃうんや」 to Haruka. Literally "You are not a person from here anymore." It's very painful. My draft: "You're not one of us anymore." But it sounds like a movie. Ideas?

"You don't belong to this place now." Hmm, closer. Or "You're not from here anymore." The simple one is the most painful, I think. Simple and cruel. Like the father. Thank you, I'll use "You're not from here anymore."
Also, a question about numbers. In the book there are many measurements in Japanese units, like 反 for field area and 貫 for weight. Should I convert to metric? Imperial? Keep Japanese?

I like your idea: keep 反 only when it's important for the farmers' way of thinking, and convert to approximate English expressions in other places, like "a few acres" — but British readers use acres for land? Yes, for farmland, acres is still common. Okay.
Thank you. Back to chapter 5. The sea is calling, as Kawabe-sensei would say. Actually she would not say this, it is a cliché, she would hate it.
Hello! Two updates, both about life.

First, Aoi's wedding — I said 11 April before, but it's actually 18 April. Aoi changed it in the summer because the hall was available on the 18th with the garden room, and I didn't update my calendar. She was very angry that I had the wrong date in my head, "you are giving the SPEECH, onee-chan!". So: 18 April 2027, Kamogawa Garden Hall, Kyoto.

Second, I decided to move! I signed a contract for a 2LDK in Suita, near Esaka station. The move is on 28 November. One room will be my office, with a door, so Mochi cannot come to the keyboard (she will scream at the door, I know).

I'm sad to leave Tenma and the tofu man, but the space and the rent are better. The new place is managed by a company called Midori Housing, my contact is Ms. Ueno. So after the move, no more kind Mr. Okada, now a company with forms for everything. I will miss him.
Until the move, I'm still in my small Tenma apartment, working on the folding table.

Can you help me make a moving checklist for Japan? Address change at the ward office, electricity, gas, water, internet, post office forwarding, My Number card address, bank, and so on. And for a freelancer, anything special? Like my business registration address for tax?
Oh, the 開業届 address change for the tax office, I forgot. And my clients' invoices, I need to update my address for Harbor Lane and Pinecone. Good list, thank you.
Moving with a cat, any tips? Mochi hates the carrier more than anything in the world.

Leave the carrier open in the room for a week before with a blanket and treats, so it's not "the scary box". And on moving day, put her in the bathroom with the door closed before the movers come. Then the new apartment: one room first, then slowly the rest. Okay. Poor Mochi.
Internet: in Japan it can take 3–4 weeks to install fibre in a new apartment. I can't be without internet for work. What should I do?
Yes, I will apply now for the installation date, and buy a pocket Wi-Fi rental for the gap. Clever.
Thank you. Lots of things to do. I make a spreadsheet tonight.

Hello. Pinecone sent the official Statement of Work for Lantern Keeper. I'll upload it. Elin also answered my question: they want American English for the game, because most of their players are in North America. So: book in British English, game in American English. My spellchecker will have an identity crisis.
Can you read the SOW and tell me if something is unusual? Especially revision rounds and payment.
Okay, so per-word rate, max three revision rounds included, extra work hourly, payment net 30. And the string freeze date and final delivery. Nothing strange, you say. Good.

Hmm, but the SOW still doesn't say anything about access to the build. Elin said "we're working on it" in her email. Without the build I'm still guessing who speaks to whom. That is still the problem for the game.

Here is an example of why I need context. These are five strings from the spreadsheet, can you see the problem?

ID 1042: 「行ってくるね」
ID 1043: 「気をつけて」
ID 1044: 「…また？」
ID 1045: 「ニャー」
ID 1046: 「灯りを頼んだぞ」

Who says what? Is 1044 the cat being sarcastic or the grandfather? Is 1046 the grandfather to the girl, or the girl to the cat (that would be funny)?

Exactly. "Again?" could be annoyed, worried, or a joke, and the English would be very different. And 「頼んだぞ」 is masculine and a bit old-fashioned, so probably the grandfather, but the director told me the cat talks like an old samurai sometimes. I can't know without seeing.
I will send Elin these five strings as an example. Concrete examples convince producers better than complaints, I think.
Also, how do I handle character limits in UI? Some strings have a 24 character limit, and English is longer than Japanese.
Yes, abbreviations carefully, and ask if the font can be smaller for some menus, and keep a list of strings that don't fit to discuss with the team. Okay. Thank you.

YES. Elin sent the build! She gave me a Steam developer key and a short video of the main story with the director talking over it. Now I know who says what. 1044 was the cat. Sarcastic. 1046 was the grandfather. And the cat really does talk like an old samurai sometimes. I'm laughing alone in my apartment.
So the game is unblocked now. I played for two hours "for research". Very important research.

Another update from Elin: the director added a new side story with a fisherman and his daughter, so the word count goes up. The new count in the spreadsheet is 55,000 words instead of 48,000. She asked me if that's okay for the schedule.

Can you help me reply? I want to say yes, it's okay for the schedule, but I also need to mention the extra cost politely, following the SOW. I don't want to be the translator who surprises them with a big invoice later.
Good, I like "as per section 2.2 of the SOW" with the calculation, very clear, no emotion. Swedish people like clear, I think.

Now a creative problem. The cat's name in Japanese is 「おもち」, which is funny because my own cat is Mochi! (Coincidence, I promise.) In English, should the cat be "Omochi", "Mochi", or something translated like "Dumpling" or "Rice Cake"?

Hmm, "Mochi" is known to many English-speaking gamers already, short and cute, and keeping it gives a little Japanese flavor. "Rice Cake" sounds like a diet snack. Okay, I'll suggest "Mochi" to Elin. My Mochi will be famous.
And the samurai-style speech of the cat — in English how do I make an old-fashioned warrior voice without being too much like a bad movie?

Yes, formal grammar, "thou" no, but maybe "Hmph. You are late, young keeper." Short, proud sentences, some old words like "indeed" and "foolish". And the joke is when the cat says something very modern in the same voice. I love it.
Thank you! Back to "research" (playing).

Hello. The novel. Still no answer from Ms. Fujimori about the dialect questions. It's been almost three weeks. I sent a polite reminder. I can translate around the problem parts, but I need the answers before I deliver the first half on the 15th. So this is what is blocking the novel now.

Here is the passage from chapter 5 that I'm most worried about, with the "trees remember the salt" phrase. If it is a local saying, my translation should sound like a saying; if it is Kawabe-sensei's image, it should sound fresh. Here is my draft:

"Grandmother said the trees remembered the salt. She said it the way other people said it might rain, without looking up from her work, her hands moving through the leaves to find the fruit by touch. Haruka had heard it all her childhood and never asked what it meant. Now, standing in the lowest terrace with the wind coming straight off the water, she thought she understood. The trees nearest the sea were smaller than the others, their trunks bent landward, their leaves thicker and darker, as if they had grown a kind of skin. Their fruit was smaller too, but sweeter. Everyone said so. The Osaka buyers paid more for the mikan from the bottom terrace, though they never came to see the trees, and if they had come they would have seen only small, crooked, ugly trees and wondered why.

'They remember,' Grandmother said again, behind her. 'Every storm. Every typhoon. They keep it in here.' She knocked on a trunk with her knuckle, twice, as if knocking on a door. 'That's why they're sweet. Sweetness is what's left over.'

Haruka wanted to ask: left over from what? But Grandmother had already moved on to the next tree, and the question went where all her questions in this place seemed to go, out over the water, and didn't come back."

Thank you for saying it is beautiful, I am blushing. And yes, I agree "Sweetness is what's left over" works in both cases: as a saying or as her own philosophy. But if it is a known saying I want to add a short note in the translator's afterword. So I still need the answer.
How long is normal for an agent to reply in Japanese publishing? Am I impatient?

Okay, a few weeks is normal, especially if the author is writing a new book. Kawabe-sensei is writing her next novel, Ms. Fujimori said. I'll be patient but I'll mention the 15 November deadline gently in the reminder. Already did. Okay.
Different question. For the translator's afterword, how long is typical, and what should be in it? Grace said I can write one, about 1,000 words.
Good: a bit about the region, dialect choices, a few words I kept in Japanese and why, and something personal but short. Not a lecture. Okay.
Thank you. Now I take Mochi to the vet for her yearly check. She is screaming in the carrier already, and we have not left the apartment.

Hello. I wrote the first draft of my speech for Aoi's wedding. I timed it reading aloud: about 5 minutes. Here it is, mixed Japanese and English. Can you tell me what to cut and if the English part sounds natural?

「皆様、本日はお忙しい中、妹・葵と ダニエルさんの結婚披露宴にお越しいただき、誠にありがとうございます。新婦の姉の由紀と申します。」

"Good afternoon everyone. My name is Yuki, I am Aoi's older sister. For our guests from Hamburg: welcome to Japan, and welcome to our family. I'm going to speak in two languages today, so if you don't understand one part, please smile and nod. That's what I did for two years when I studied in London.

When Aoi was six years old, she decided she wanted to climb the persimmon tree in our grandparents' garden in Nara. Everyone said she was too small. She climbed it anyway, got stuck at the top, and refused to come down until our grandfather promised her she could keep every persimmon she could reach. She came down with eleven persimmons and a very proud face. I think that is Aoi: she climbs first and thinks later, and somehow it always works.

So of course she met Daniel at a climbing gym."

「ダニエルさんに初めて会った時、とても背が高くて、とても礼儀正しくて、日本語で一生懸命自己紹介してくれました。『はじめまして、ダニエルです。葵さんの…えーと…ボーイフレンドです』と。その『えーと』の間に、私はこの人はいい人だと思いました。」

"Daniel, you have learned so much Japanese. But I want to teach you one more word today: 'onee-chan', big sister. Because from today, I am your onee-chan too. That means I will give you advice you didn't ask for, I will call you when I can't open a jar, and I will always, always be on your side. Except when you are wrong. Then I will be on Aoi's side.

Aoi, you were always the brave one. I was the one who read books under the tree while you climbed it. But you always came down and told me what you saw from the top. Thank you for that, and for letting me share your view of the world.

To both of you: may your life together be like that tree. Strong roots, lots of fruit, and always something exciting to climb."

「どうぞ末永くお幸せに。本日は本当におめでとうございます。」

Oh, you're right, "Except when you are wrong. Then I will be on Aoi's side" is funny but I should keep it, it's the best joke. And the jar line. Maybe I cut the London part, nobody cares about my studies. And shorten the Japanese part about meeting Daniel.
Hmm, wait, "may your life together be like that tree... always something exciting to climb" — is there anything bad there for 忌み言葉? "Fall" is not in it. Good. Climbing is going up, it's lucky.
How long should a sister's speech normally be at a Japanese reception? Aoi didn't tell me a limit yet. The wedding planner will send a schedule.
Okay, usually around 3 minutes for friends and family speeches. So I should cut maybe 2 minutes. Ugh. I'll wait for the planner's schedule and then cut. Keep this version for now.
Thank you. I cried a little writing the tree part. Mochi looked at me like I'm crazy.
Hello. A lazy Sunday for me. Only questions for fun today.

I want to cook something nice for myself tonight. I have salmon, spinach, rice, miso, and some shiitake. Something Japanese-Western fusion? And remember: no buckwheat for me. (I know there is no buckwheat in my fridge, but just reminding you.)
Miso butter salmon with sautéed spinach and shiitake on rice, so good. Butter and miso is my favourite combination. Thank you.
Can you recommend a novel in English by a Japanese author translated by a really good translator? I want to study how others solve problems. Not Murakami, I know his translators already.

Oh, "The Memory Police" by Ogawa Yoko, translated by Stephen Snyder, and "Convenience Store Woman" by Murata Sayaka translated by Ginny Tapley Takemori. I read Convenience Store Woman in Japanese but never in English. I'll read it in English and compare. Good homework.

Also, I'm thinking of making a small blog about translation, in English, for other translators and readers. Here is my draft for the "About" page, is it okay?

"Hello, I'm Yuki. I translate Japanese literature and games into English, and sometimes English into Japanese, from my small apartment in Osaka, usually with a cat on my keyboard. I started translating because I loved reading in two languages and I was always frustrated that my friends abroad couldn't read the books I loved. Now I try to build small bridges, one sentence at a time.

On this blog I will write about the problems I meet in my work: words that don't exist in English, jokes that die at the border, dialects, honorifics, and the strange feeling of living inside someone else's book for months. I will also share what I am reading and learning. I am not an academic, I am a working translator, so this will be practical, sometimes messy, and hopefully a little funny.

If you are a translator, a reader, or just curious about how Japanese becomes English, welcome. Please make yourself at home. The cat will move eventually."
Thank you! I will change "from my small apartment in Osaka" because I'm moving soon, and maybe "in Osaka" is enough. And "The cat will move eventually" stays, it's true.
Can you suggest five first blog post topics? Practical and interesting.

"Five Japanese words I refuse to translate (and why)" is a good one, and "What a cat in a video game taught me about voice" — but I can't write about Lantern Keeper until the release, it's confidential. I'll save it for March.
Okay, thank you. Good Sunday.

Hello. The wedding planner sent the schedule notes for Aoi's wedding. Her name is Ms. Hirano, very professional. I'll upload them. There is a lot of information and Aoi said "onee-chan, please read everything, you are the organised one". I am not the organised one, I just pretend.
Can you check what I personally need to do? I see my name in a few places.
Okay, so I'm also helping with the reception guests from Germany, and there's a rehearsal the day before. I didn't know about that, good that I read it.
And I need to send my speech text to Ms. Hirano in advance, for the interpreter? Ah no, it says for the MC to know the timing. Okay.
Do I need to prepare 御祝儀 (the money gift) even though I'm the sister and helping? How much is normal for a sibling?

I see, for siblings it's usually more than for friends, often 50,000 or 100,000 yen depending on age and situation, and some families agree on a different arrangement. I'll ask my mother what our family does. She will have an opinion, she always has an opinion.
Daniel's parents asked Aoi what they should wear as the groom's parents. They are German, they want to respect the culture. What would you suggest?

Formal dark suit for the father and a formal dress for the mother, avoid white and avoid too much black (black dress alone looks like a funeral, but black with colourful accessories is fine). I'll tell Aoi.
Thank you. Wedding planning is a full-time job, and I already have two jobs.
Hello. Today just a quick question and then work.
My speech is 5 minutes. The planner says 3 minutes maximum, including translation. Help me. Which parts do I cut?

Okay, cut the London joke, shorten the Daniel meeting part to one sentence in Japanese, and do the "onee-chan" part only in English with one Japanese line. Keep the persimmon tree story and the tree ending. That's a good plan. I'll try to rewrite it this weekend.
Back to work. Lantern Keeper. I'm translating the item descriptions now. There is an item called 「ひだまりのランタン」. Literally "Lantern of the sunny spot". Hmm. Ideas?
"Sunpatch Lantern" is cute! Or "Sunny Nook Lantern". I like "Sunpatch". It sounds like something a cat would sleep in. Perfect for this game.
And this one: 「こたつの記憶」 — "Memory of the Kotatsu". Should I explain kotatsu or keep it? American players may not know.

Hmm, keep "kotatsu" because many gamers know it from anime, and the description text can show what it is: "a warm table with a blanket, where everyone gathers in winter". Good, the description does the explaining.
Thank you. I'm at 22,000 words for the game now. Good pace.
Oh, and still nothing from Ms. Fujimori. Every morning I check my email first thing. Nothing. Okay. Patience.
Hello. I need to vent a little. Is that okay?

I'm tired. Two big projects, the move, the wedding speech, and the dialect questions for the novel are still unanswered. Some days I feel like a juggler with too many balls, and the cat is also one of the balls.
Thank you, yes, I know it's temporary. After December 18 the game is finished, after January 31 the novel is finished, and the move is November 28. In February I can breathe. Maybe I go to an onsen.
Can you recommend an onsen town near Osaka that's not too touristy, for a quiet two nights in February? I want to read and soak and not speak to anyone.

Kinosaki is lovely but busy, and Arima is close but touristy. Yunomine in Wakayama is small and quiet and very old. Wakayama! The same region as the novel. That's fate. I'll go there after the novel is finished and look at the sea and the mikan trees.
Ah, but I need to be careful with food in ryokan, sometimes they serve soba. I'll tell them about the buckwheat allergy when I book. Thank you for reminding me before I remembered.

Also, Kitsune Comics emailed again about the manga. They are asking for an answer by the end of October. I still don't know. If I say yes, it starts in March. Money is good to have, but I want to rest in February. Still thinking.
Can you help me write a reply that says I'm interested but need until the end of October to decide, without sounding like I'm playing games?
Perfect, honest and short. Sent.
Thank you for listening. I feel better. Mochi is sitting on my notes now, so I think it's break time anyway.

Hello. Tax time is not yet, but I want to prepare. Let me paste my rough income list for this year so far, to see if I need to pay estimated tax or anything:

January: technical manual translation (Tokyo client) 180,000 yen
February: short story for literary magazine 60,000 yen
March: website localisation (Osaka hotel) 240,000 yen
April: technical manual (same Tokyo client) 150,000 yen
May: subtitle translation (documentary) 210,000 yen
June: interpretation at trade fair, 3 days 165,000 yen
July: Harbor Lane first instalment (one third of estimated fee) about 2,913 pounds, received in August, approx 560,000 yen
August: website updates (hotel) 80,000 yen
September: nothing big, small jobs 45,000 yen
October onward: Pinecone 50% on first delivery (December), maybe Harbor Lane second instalment after 15 November delivery

Ah, so in Japan I may need to pay 予定納税 (prepaid tax) next year if this year's tax is high enough, but not now. And I should keep all the invoices and the bank records showing the exchange rate on the day I received the pounds. Okay.
Can I deduct my new apartment's work room as a business expense? Like a percentage of the rent?

Yes, a reasonable proportion for the work room, like by floor area, if I really use it only for work. And part of internet and electricity. Mochi does not count as a business expense, sadly, even though she is my "supervisor".
What about the cost of moving? Can I deduct part of it?
Hmm, probably only the part related to moving business equipment, and it's a grey area. I'll ask my accountant friend. Thank you.
Different question: is it worth registering for the invoice system (インボイス制度) as a freelancer if most of my clients are foreign? I registered last year because Japanese clients asked.
Okay, for foreign clients it doesn't matter much, but for Japanese clients it does, so keep it. Fine.
Thank you. Boring but important.
Hello! ANSWERS ARRIVED? No. Not yet. I just wanted to say hello. Ha.

Actually, a real question: I'm preparing the glossary for the novel. There are many words related to mikan farming. Here is my list, can you check my English choices make sense for British readers?

摘果 (tekika) - fruit thinning
剪定 (sentei) - pruning
段々畑 (dandan-batake) - terraced fields / terraces
石垣 (ishigaki) - stone walls (of the terraces)
早生みかん (wase mikan) - early-ripening mikan
貯蔵庫 (chozōko) - storage shed / fruit store
選果場 (senkajō) - fruit-sorting house / packing house
農協 (nōkyō) - the agricultural co-op
防風林 (bōfūrin) - windbreak trees
台風 (taifū) - typhoon
軽トラ (keitora) - light truck / kei truck
もんぺ (monpe) - work trousers / monpe

Good. "Packing house" is more natural than "fruit-sorting house". And for 軽トラ, in the opening I used "light truck" already, keep it consistent. And "monpe" — explain once and then keep? Or "work trousers" always? I think "work trousers", it's not important enough to keep in Japanese.
And "the co-op" for 農協 is perfect. British readers know co-op from the supermarket, haha, but in context it's clear.
What do British people call the small farmer's fruit stall by the road where you leave money in a box? In Japan it's 無人販売所. There is one in the novel.
"Honesty box" or "honesty stall"! I love it. That's exactly the feeling. Honesty stall. Thank you!
One more: how do I say 「お疲れ様」 between farm workers at the end of the day, in a natural British way?

Hello. Elin sent feedback on my first 200 sample strings for the game. Mostly good, but some comments I don't fully understand. Can you help me interpret? Here is her email:

"Hi Yuki! Thanks so much for the sample batch, the team loved it. Some notes below, nothing major:
1. Overall tone: spot on for the main character. The cat is a HIT, our QA lead laughed out loud at 'Hmph. The sea does not wait for sleepy keepers.' Keep going in that direction.
2. Grandfather: a few lines feel a bit too formal/stiff for a warm grandpa ('I am grateful for your assistance' -> maybe 'Thanks, kiddo' or similar?). In the JP he's gruff but loving. We want players to feel the love under the gruffness.
3. UI: 'Inventory' should be 'Satchel' per our glossary (sorry, glossary v1.1 was missing this, attached v1.2). Also 'Save Game' -> 'Rest at the Lighthouse'. We like diegetic UI.
4. Tutorial text: please keep instructions max 2 short sentences per popup. Our playtesters skip anything longer. Imperative mood, second person ('Tap the lantern to light it.').
5. Item descriptions: love the 'Sunpatch Lantern'! For flavor text we're happy with a bit of whimsy, max 140 characters.
6. Achievement names: puns are welcome! But please avoid puns that only work in English if the achievement icon shows something specific - we'll send icons next week.
7. Capitalization: our style guide says title case for item names and sentence case for everything else, I noticed a few inconsistencies, no worries.
8. Spelling: just a reminder we're US English, I saw 'colour' once in the sample (we've all been there!).
Looking forward to the next batch! Elin"

Oh no, "colour". The novel is infecting the game. Yes. Two documents open at the same time is dangerous. I'll set different spellcheck languages per file and maybe use different fonts so my eyes know which world I'm in.
"Diegetic UI" — what is that?
Ah, UI that exists inside the story world, like "Satchel" instead of "Inventory", "Rest at the Lighthouse" instead of "Save". The player stays inside the fantasy. Clever.
For the grandfather: in Japanese he says 「助かったぞ」. "Thanks, kiddo" is a bit too American-cute? Ideas for gruff but loving?
"You did good, little keeper." or "Not bad. Not bad at all." I like the second, very grandfather. Thank you.
Also, how do you say "thank you" and "good morning" in Swedish? I want to write something small to Elin at the end of my emails, just to be friendly.
"Tack!" and "God morgon!" — and "Tack så mycket" for thank you very much. And "fika" is the coffee break culture. Cute. I'll sign the next email "Tack så mycket! / Yuki". She will like it, I hope.
Thank you. Back to work.

Hello. My friend Saki is studying for JLPT N1, she's Taiwanese, lives in Osaka. She asked me a grammar question I can't explain well even though I'm native. Can you help me explain the difference between 「〜わけにはいかない」 and 「〜ざるを得ない」?

Yes, わけにはいかない = "I can't do it (because of social/moral reasons)", ざるを得ない = "I have no choice but to do it". Opposite directions in a way. Good examples with the boss and the drinking party. Saki will love it.
And 「〜っぽい」 vs 「〜らしい」 vs 「〜みたい」? She is confused about all three.
That's a very clear table. Especially らしい meaning "typical of" as in 「子供らしい」, which is different from "seems like". I'll send it to her.

She also asked me to check her English cover letter, she's applying to a hotel job in Umeda that needs English and Japanese. Here it is:

"Dear Hiring Manager,
I am writing to apply for the position of Guest Relations Staff at your hotel, as advertised on your website. I am from Taiwan and I have lived in Osaka for four years. I can speak Mandarin (native), Japanese (JLPT N2, studying for N1), and English (TOEIC 865).

Hello. I'm thinking of applying for a translation grant for my next project after the novel, maybe a short story collection by another author I love. There is a grant for literary translation from Japanese. Here are the guidelines, can you summarise what I need?

"Literary Translation Support Programme - Guidelines for Applicants
Purpose: The programme supports the translation and publication of Japanese literary works in other languages, in order to promote understanding of Japanese culture abroad.
Eligibility: Applications must be submitted by a publisher outside Japan that intends to publish the translated work. Individual translators cannot apply directly, but the translator's qualifications are evaluated as part of the application. The work must be a Japanese literary work (fiction, poetry, essays, or literary non-fiction) that has not previously been published in the target language.

Hello. A small personal project: I want to write some travel memories in English to practise more creative writing. Here's a short piece about a trip to Hokkaido two winters ago. Please correct only grammar and very unnatural phrases, I want to keep my voice:

"In February two years ago I went to Hokkaido alone. Everyone asked me why alone, as if travelling alone is a kind of illness. I wanted silence, and snow is the best silence in the world.

I took the night ferry from Maizuru to Otaru, because I am afraid of airplanes a little and because I wanted to arrive slowly. The ferry was almost empty. Truck drivers in the public bath, a family with a very small child who cried all night, and me. In the morning the sea was grey and flat like a sheet of metal, and then suddenly Otaru appeared, white and quiet, like someone had erased the colour from the town.

I stayed three days in a small inn near the canal. The owner was an old woman who spoke very fast in Hokkaido dialect and laughed at everything I said, even when I said nothing funny. She gave me hot milk every night before bed. I don't usually drink milk but I drank it every night because it felt like a ritual.

On the second day I walked to the end of the canal and sat on a bench covered in snow, which was a mistake for my trousers. I watched the snow fall into the water and disappear immediately. Thousands and thousands of snowflakes, each one perfect and unique, as the children's books say, disappearing in one second without any sound. I thought it was sad. Then I thought, no, it's not sad, the water is just made of all the snow that fell before. Nothing disappears, it only changes.

I think about that bench often. When I translate, sometimes I feel like the snowflakes, every Japanese word disappearing into the English. But maybe the English is made of them. Nothing disappears, it only changes.

On the last night the old woman gave me a small bag of dried squid for the ferry. I still don't know why dried squid. But I ate all of it."

Thank you! Very few corrections, I'm proud. "Which was a mistake for my trousers" stays, you said it's funny in a good way. And "like someone had erased the colour from the town", you suggested "drained", but I think "erased" is more my feeling. I keep "erased".
Wait, "colour" — this is a personal piece, so I can use British or American? Ha. I'll use British, I like the u.
Do you think I could publish this on my blog? Or is it too personal?
Okay, it's personal but not private. And it connects to translation at the end, so it fits the blog. Maybe my second post.
Thank you. I feel like a writer today, not only a translator.

Hello. Still no answers from Ms. Fujimori. I sent a second reminder yesterday, in Japanese this time, very polite keigo. The 15 November delivery is getting closer. I'm translating around the dialect parts and marking them yellow.

Here is a passage from chapter 8 where the mother speaks standard Japanese and the father speaks dialect, in the same scene. I made the difference visible in English, but I'm not sure if it's too subtle or too strong. Can you look?

"Her mother set the teapot down between them with the care of someone placing a stone on a grave. 'Your father thinks you should stay until the harvest is finished,' she said. 'I think you should decide for yourself.' She said it in the clean, careful Japanese of the city she had left thirty years ago, each word placed where it belonged, and Haruka understood that this, too, was a kind of argument.

From the doorway her father said, 'Harvest's not finished till it's finished.' He didn't come in. He stood with one hand on the frame, his boots still on, the way he always stood when he wanted to be part of a conversation without admitting it. 'Bottom terrace is still to do. And the Ishida boy's useless.'

'The Ishida boy is nineteen,' her mother said, without turning round.

'Nineteen's old enough to be useful.'

'You were useless at nineteen.'

'And look at me now.' He went back out. They heard the truck start, and stall, and start again.

Her mother poured the tea. 'He's frightened,' she said, very quietly, in a voice that was almost dialect, almost from here, as if for a moment the thirty years had worn through. 'He won't say it. But he is.'

Haruka looked at the steam rising from her cup and did not ask what he was frightened of. She thought she knew. She thought it was the same thing she was frightened of, which was that she would stay, and that she would not."

Thank you. So the contrast works through sentence length and contractions: the mother's sentences complete and careful, the father's clipped and missing subjects ("Bottom terrace is still to do", "Nineteen's old enough"). And the moment when the mother's voice becomes "almost dialect" — in English I show it only by the narration, not by changing her words. You think that's the right choice?

Yes, I agree, if I suddenly change her English it will look strange. The narration carries it. Good. But I still want Kawabe-sensei's answer about whether the mother's standard Japanese is intentional, my question number 5. I'm 95% sure, but 95% is not 100%.
Do you think I should ask Grace to contact Ms. Fujimori too? The contract says the Publisher will facilitate communication where necessary.

Hello. Kitsune Comics sent me a sample page script to translate as a test, "no pressure, just to see the style fit". Original (simplified for you):
Panel 1: (Rin, at the school gate, sees Kaito with a cat) 「え、その猫どうしたの？」
Panel 2: Kaito: 「知らない。ついてきた」

Panel 5: Rin: 「…完全にあんたの猫じゃん」 / Kaito: 「違う」
Panel 6: (Small panel, cat looking at Kaito) Caption: 「その日から、猫は違わなかった。」

My translation:
Panel 1: Rin: "Wait, what's with the cat?"
Panel 2: Kaito: "No idea. It followed me."
Panel 3: Rin: "Followed you... home?" / Kaito: "Probably."
Panel 4: SFX: plop
Panel 5: Rin: "...That's totally your cat now." / Kaito: "It's not."
Panel 6: Caption: "From that day on, it was."

And the last caption! The Japanese is a joke: 「猫は違わなかった」 = "the cat was not 'not his'". My "From that day on, it was." — you think it works because English readers will connect it with "It's not"? Yes, I hope so.
