Hello. Elin sent the updated Pinecone style guide, version 1.2. It's long and I want to make a short checklist from it that I can keep next to my screen. Here's the main part:

"PINECONE GAMES - LOCALIZATION STYLE GUIDE v1.2 (EN-US)
1. Voice and tone. Lantern Keeper is a cozy, gentle game about responsibility, community and small acts of care. The English should feel warm, light and slightly whimsical, never sarcastic toward the player (characters may be sarcastic toward each other). Avoid modern slang that will date quickly ('lit', 'vibe', 'slay'). Avoid profanity entirely; the strongest permitted expressions are 'darn', 'blast' and 'oh, barnacles' (the latter reserved for Captain Ume).
2. Player address. Use second person ('you') in tutorials and system messages. Use imperative mood for instructions ('Tap the lantern to light it.'). Never use 'the player' in in-game text.
3. Character voices. Hana (protagonist): curious, earnest, short sentences, occasional self-talk. Grandpa Tetsu: gruff, few words, warm underneath; avoids direct expressions of affection but shows them through actions and small praise. Mochi (cat): pompous, archaic-sounding but never using 'thee/thou'; delivers occasional modern phrases in the same lofty tone for comic effect. Captain Ume: loud, nautical expressions, mixed metaphors. Villagers: each has a one-line description in the character sheet; keep them distinct.
4. Names. Keep Japanese personal names (Hana, Tetsu, Ume). Place names: translate descriptive names ('Kazemachi' -> 'Windtown') unless listed as 'keep' in the glossary. The cat's name is 'Mochi' in all languages.
5. Capitalization. Title Case for item names, location names and achievement names. Sentence case for UI buttons, menu labels, dialogue and descriptions. Never use ALL CAPS except for single-word shouts in dialogue ('WAIT!').
6. Punctuation. Use the serial (Oxford) comma. Use the ellipsis character (…) rather than three periods. Use em dashes without spaces. Use straight quotes in the spreadsheet; the engine converts them.
7. Numbers. Spell out one to nine in dialogue; use numerals for 10 and above, and always in UI.
8. Length. Dialogue boxes: max 3 lines of 42 characters each. Tutorial popups: max 2 sentences. Item flavor text: max 140 characters. Button labels: max 14 characters.
9. Variables. Do not translate or alter variables in curly braces ({player_name}, {count}). Make sure sentences read naturally with plural and singular values; flag strings that need plural handling.
10. Cultural references. Japanese food and objects may remain (kotatsu, onigiri, mochi) if the context makes them understandable; add a light explanation in descriptions where needed. Replace puns and wordplay with English equivalents of similar spirit rather than translating literally.
11. Queries. Log questions in the 'Queries' tab of the spreadsheet with the string ID. The team answers within 2 working days (Stockholm time).
12. Glossary. The glossary (v1.2) is mandatory. Do not invent alternative translations for glossary terms. Suggest changes in the Queries tab."
Thank you, a short checklist is exactly what I needed. "Oh, barnacles" only for Captain Ume, I love that. And the serial comma, the novel's British style doesn't always use it, so again two worlds.
Wait, rule 7: numbers one to nine spelled out in dialogue. I used "3 lanterns" in some dialogue. I'll search and fix.

And rule 6: the ellipsis character "…". In Japanese text we use 「…」 too, so that's easy. But em dashes without spaces — in the novel, Harbor Lane uses spaced en dashes, I think. I need to check with Grace. Two style guides in my head. Help.

Okay, I'll make two small cards: a blue one for the novel (British, spaced en dash, no serial comma unless needed) and a green one for the game (American, closed em dash, serial comma). Colour coding. Or "color coding" on the green card. Ha.
Can you write both cards for me, max 8 lines each?
Perfect. Printed. Taped to the left and right of my monitor. Mochi already tried to eat the green one.
Thank you, this will save me from many small mistakes.

Hello. Weekend project: I want to learn to bake bread. Japanese shokupan, the soft milk bread. I found a recipe but I don't understand some steps. Here it is:

"Hokkaido Milk Bread (Shokupan) with Tangzhong
Tangzhong: 25 g bread flour, 125 ml milk. Whisk in a small saucepan over low heat, stirring constantly, until it thickens to a paste and you can see lines when you stir (about 65°C). Cool to room temperature, cover with plastic wrap touching the surface.
Dough: 350 g bread flour, 40 g sugar, 6 g salt, 7 g instant yeast, 1 egg (about 50 g), 120 ml warm milk, all of the tangzhong, 30 g unsalted butter (softened).
1. In a large bowl or stand mixer, combine flour, sugar, salt and yeast. Add egg, milk and tangzhong. Mix until a shaggy dough forms.
2. Knead for 10 minutes until smooth, then add butter a little at a time and knead for another 10-15 minutes until the dough passes the windowpane test (a small piece can be stretched thin enough to see light through without tearing).
3. Shape into a ball, place in a lightly oiled bowl, cover and let rise in a warm place until doubled, about 60-90 minutes.
4. Punch down, divide into 3 equal pieces. Roll each piece into an oval, fold the sides into the middle, then roll up into a log. Place the three logs side by side in a greased 1 lb loaf tin (about 21 x 11 cm).
5. Cover and let rise again until the dough reaches about 1 cm below the rim of the tin, 40-60 minutes.
6. Brush with egg wash or milk. Bake at 175°C for 30-35 minutes, until golden and the internal temperature reaches about 88-90°C. Tent with foil if browning too quickly.
7. Remove from the tin immediately and cool on a rack for at least 1 hour before slicing (it will be squashed if you cut it hot)."
Thank you. So tangzhong is like a pre-cooked flour paste that holds more water, that's why the bread is so soft and stays fresh. Like magic, but science.
I don't have a stand mixer. Can I knead by hand for 25 minutes? My arms are translator arms, not baker arms.
Ha, okay, the "slap and fold" method is faster and more fun. I'll try it. Mochi will watch from the counter and judge me.
Is there anything in this recipe I need to check for my buckwheat allergy? Bread flour is wheat, right?

Yes, bread flour is wheat, no buckwheat. But I should check the packaging for "may contain buckwheat" because some Japanese flour mills process soba flour on the same lines. Good point, I didn't think about that. I'll check the label.
My oven is a small microwave-oven combination. Will that work?
Okay, it works but I should preheat well, and maybe lower the temperature by 10 degrees and check earlier, because small ovens are hot near the top. And the 1 lb tin must fit. I'll measure tomorrow.
Thank you! If it works I'll take a slice to the tofu man as part of my goodbye. Bread and tofu, strange combination, but made with love.

Hello. For the future (maybe 2027), I want to pitch a short story collection to publishers. The author is Morioka Natsu, she writes very short, strange stories about everyday life in Osaka. Nobody has translated her yet. I translated one story as a sample. Can you read it and tell me if it would catch an English editor's attention? It's short:

"The Umbrella Office

On the third floor of a building near Tenma station, between a dentist and a company that sells industrial adhesives, there is an office that collects lost umbrellas. It has no sign. You find it only if you are looking for something else.

Mr. Kuroda has worked there for twenty-two years. Every morning at eight he receives the umbrellas the trains have left behind: the transparent ones, which are most of them, and the few others - a black one with a carved wooden handle, a child's yellow one with ducks, a man's folding umbrella still in its sleeve, as if its owner never believed it would rain. He writes each one in a ledger. Date. Line. Colour. Special features. Then he hangs it on one of the long metal rails that fill the room, row after row, so that walking between them is like walking through a forest that has decided to stand very still.

Almost nobody comes to collect their umbrella. A transparent umbrella costs five hundred yen; a train ticket to the office costs more. After three months the umbrellas are given to a recycling company, and the rails are filled again. Mr. Kuroda does not mind. He says the umbrellas are not really lost. They are only waiting, and waiting is not the same thing.

Once, ten years ago, a woman came for the black umbrella with the wooden handle. She was perhaps seventy. She said it had belonged to her husband, who had died the spring before, and that she had left it on the Keihan line by mistake, and that she had been looking for it for four months, at every station office, until someone told her about this place. Mr. Kuroda found it in the ledger, then on the rail, and brought it to her. She did not open it. She held it against her chest, the way you would hold a sleeping cat, and thanked him, and left.

Mr. Kuroda thinks about her sometimes, when it rains. He thinks that most things that are lost are not looked for, and that this is not sad, exactly, but that it makes the things that are looked for very important. He thinks he would like to be looked for like that umbrella, one day. Not by many people. By one person would be enough.

In the afternoon he eats his lunch at his desk, rice balls from the convenience store downstairs, and listens to the rain on the window, and counts, without meaning to, the people passing below who have forgotten their umbrellas and are walking quickly, heads down, through the wet streets of the city, toward whatever they are hurrying to, believing that they have lost nothing at all."
Thank you! You think the last sentence is the strongest, and the "forest that has decided to stand very still" image. I'm happy. Editors like a strong last line.
And you're right, "Special features" in the ledger is a little joke that I want to keep, it's like a product description for umbrellas.
Now the pitch letter to an editor. Should I write to Grace first, since I already work with Harbor Lane? Or is that unprofessional while I'm still working on the novel?

Okay, it's actually normal to mention it to your current editor, as long as I don't distract from the current project. Maybe after I deliver the first half, so she sees I'm reliable first. Smart timing.

Can you help me draft a short pitch? Not to send now, just to have ready. Include: who the author is, why she's special, the collection (14 stories, about 45,000 words in English), that rights are available as far as I know, and that I can send the sample.

Good. Short and clear. "Morioka writes about the overlooked corners of Osaka with the precision of a poet and the timing of a comedian" — a little bit marketing, but editors like a one-line hook. I'll keep it.
How do I check if the English rights are really available? I don't want to promise something false.

Contact her Japanese publisher's rights department, or her agent if she has one, and ask directly whether English rights are available and whether a sample translation can be shown to publishers. Okay, I'll do that in January when I have time to breathe.
Thank you. I feel excited about the future, even though the present is very busy.

Hello, a small English question. A friend sent me a poem she wrote in English for her grandmother's 90th birthday and asked me if the English is natural. I'm not a poetry expert, but can you look?

"Ninety winters on your hands,
ninety springs inside your laugh,
you taught me how to fold a crane
and how to cut an apple in half
so that the star inside shows through -
a secret only grandmas knew.
You never said the word for love,
you said, 'Have you eaten yet?'
and filled my bowl before I asked,
and that is how I won't forget:
not in words, but rice and tea,
the way you always cared for me."

Oh, it's lovely. The apple star and "Have you eaten yet?" — that's so true for Asian grandmothers. You say the only small thing is the rhythm in line 4, "and how to cut an apple in half" has one extra beat. Maybe "and cut an apple clean in half"? That keeps the rhyme with "laugh" and fixes the beat.
And "a secret only grandmas knew" — is "grandmas" too casual for a poem?
Okay, casual is fine because the whole poem is warm and simple. It fits. I'll tell her: change line 4 a little, everything else, don't touch. She'll be happy.
Thank you. Poetry is the hardest translation, even when it's already in English.

Oh, one more question about the poem. My friend wants to also make a Japanese version for her grandmother, who doesn't read English. She asked me to translate it, but keep it simple, not too literary, because her grandmother likes plain words. Should I keep the rhyme in Japanese? Japanese poetry doesn't usually rhyme.

Yes, I agree: no rhyme, but keep the rhythm with a 7-5 feeling where natural, and keep the images exactly: the crane, the apple star, 「ご飯食べた？」. The images are the poem, not the rhyme. I'll try tonight after work, it's a nice small gift to make.
Thank you. Good night, and Mochi says good night (she is asleep, as always).
Hello, one small question. In English, when do you write "Ms" and when "Ms."? I see both in emails from Grace and from Elin and I'm confused.

Ah, British English usually no full stop (Ms, Mr, Dr) and American English with a full stop (Ms., Mr., Dr.). So again British for the novel, American for the game. My two worlds even in the titles. Okay, I'll add it to my blue and green cards.
And "Mx"? I saw it in a form recently.
I see, a gender-neutral title. Good to know, I'll be careful to use what people prefer. Thank you!

Hello. Something is bothering me. A Japanese client, the Tokyo technical manual company, asked me if I can do "MTPE" — machine translation post-editing — for half my normal rate. They say the AI does most of the work. I want to understand the situation better before I answer. A colleague sent me this article, what do you think, is it fair?

"The Translator's Dilemma: Post-Editing and the Future of the Profession
Over the past few years, machine translation has improved dramatically, particularly for language pairs with large amounts of training data. For many types of commercial content - product descriptions, technical documentation, internal communications - machine output is now often usable as a first draft. As a result, many language service providers have shifted towards 'machine translation post-editing' (MTPE) workflows, in which a human translator reviews and corrects machine output instead of translating from scratch.
Proponents argue that MTPE increases productivity, reduces costs for clients and allows translators to handle larger volumes. Some studies report productivity gains of 30 to 50 percent for certain text types. Critics point out that these gains vary enormously depending on the content, the language pair and the quality of the machine output. For language pairs with very different structures, such as Japanese and English, machine output may contain subtle errors in meaning, register and coherence that are harder to detect than obvious mistakes, and post-editing can take almost as long as translation.
Translators also report that post-editing is cognitively different from translating. Rather than creating a text, they are constantly evaluating someone else's choices, which some describe as more tiring and less satisfying. There is also a risk of 'priming': exposure to the machine's wording can make translators accept awkward or inaccurate phrasing they would never have produced themselves.
Rates for MTPE are often set at 50 to 70 percent of standard translation rates, based on the assumption of higher productivity. Translators argue that rates should instead reflect the actual effort required, which can only be assessed by examining the specific content. Professional associations recommend that translators evaluate a sample of machine output before agreeing to an MTPE rate, and that clients and translators agree in advance on the expected quality level: 'light' post-editing (making the text understandable and accurate) is very different from 'full' post-editing (making it indistinguishable from human translation).
For literary translation, the consensus among practitioners remains that machine translation is of limited use, as the work depends on voice, rhythm, ambiguity and cultural nuance. However, publishers are watching developments closely, and some have experimented with machine-assisted workflows for genre fiction.
Ultimately, the profession is likely to divide: high-volume, low-visibility content will increasingly be handled by machine-plus-human workflows, while high-value content, including marketing, legal, medical and literary texts, will continue to require skilled human translators - who may also use machine tools as one resource among many."

So: ask for a sample of their machine output first, clarify light vs full post-editing, and set the rate based on real effort, not an automatic 50%. For technical manuals Japanese to English, the machine output is probably decent for simple parts and bad for complex warnings. Okay.
Can you help me write a reply to the client? Professional, open to trying, but I want to test a sample first.
Good. I like "I'm happy to explore this, and to make sure the quality stays where your customers expect it, I'd like to evaluate a 1,000-word sample first." Calm, not defensive.
Honestly, does this worry you for my future? Should I worry?
Thank you. Literary and games are the human-voice side, so I'm in a good place. And using tools for terminology and consistency is fine. I'll keep the technical client but not depend on it.
Okay, enough serious thinking. What's a good, simple dinner for a tired person? Fish, vegetables, rice — no buckwheat, and nothing that needs more than one pan.
Salmon and mushroom takikomi gohan in the rice cooker! Zero pans! Genius. Thank you.

Hello. Moving preparation. I'm throwing away things before the move. Osaka has strict garbage rules for big items, 粗大ごみ. Here's my list of things I want to get rid of, can you help me sort into: big garbage (needs reservation and sticker), normal garbage, recycling, or sell/give away?

- old folding table (my current desk!)
- futon (old, 7 years)
- small bookshelf, wood, 90 cm
- broken electric kettle
- 40 old paperback books in English and Japanese
- an old laptop (2016)
- winter coat I never wear
- cat tower that Mochi never used (she prefers boxes)
- printer that only prints in pink
- 6 empty wine bottles
- old curtains (the new apartment has different window sizes)
- a big plastic storage box, cracked
- desk lamp, works fine but ugly
- 3 pairs of shoes
- old phone, 2019
- frying pan, the coating is coming off

Thank you. So the laptop and phone are under the small appliance recycling law, I must use a special collection or the ward box, and delete data first. The printer is big garbage or small appliance depending on size. And books, the second-hand bookshop or the library donation. The cat tower, I can give away on Jimoty, maybe another cat will love it.
How do I safely delete data from the old laptop? It has old client files.
Okay, a full reset with drive wipe, or if it's very old just remove the drive and destroy it. I'll take out the drive, it's easier, and smash it with a hammer. Very satisfying, I think.
For the reservation of big garbage, how early should I book in Osaka? The move is the 28th of November.
At least two weeks before, especially at the end of the month when everyone moves. I'll book this week. Thank you.
The new apartment needs curtains. In Japan, curtain sizes are standard? I measured the windows: 100 x 178 cm and 200 x 135 cm.
Yes, those are common standard sizes, I can buy ready-made at Nitori. For the work room, blackout curtains so the morning sun doesn't hit the screen. Good idea.
I'll miss this tiny apartment a little. Seven years here. Mochi came here as a kitten. Okay, I'm not crying, you are crying.

Hello. I want to write a goodbye letter to the old man at the tofu shop in Tenma shopping street. He knows Mochi's name even though he has never met her, because I talk about her all the time. I wrote it in Japanese. Can you check the feeling is right? And maybe give me an English version for my blog someday:

「豆腐屋のおじさんへ
いつも美味しいお豆腐をありがとうございます。七年間、ほぼ毎週土曜日にお店に通わせていただきました。朝早く、まだ商店街が静かな時間に、湯気の向こうからおじさんが「おはようさん、今日はモチちゃん元気か？」と声をかけてくれるのが、私の一週間で一番好きな時間でした。
来月、吹田に引っ越すことになりました。仕事部屋が欲しくて決めたのですが、天満を離れるのは本当に寂しいです。特におじさんの絹ごしと厚揚げが食べられなくなるのが一番寂しいです。
吹田からでも、たまには電車に乗って買いに来ます。その時は、モチの写真を持ってきますね。
いつまでもお元気で。
由紀」

Thank you. You say the feeling is warm and natural, good. 「通わせていただきました」 maybe a little too formal for him, he speaks Osaka-ben with everyone, but it's a letter, so a little formal is okay. I'll keep it.

And the English version: "Every Saturday morning, while the shopping street was still quiet, you'd call out through the steam, 'Morning! How's Mochi doing?'" — I love "through the steam". That's exactly the picture.
Should I bring a small gift with the letter? What's appropriate?
A small box of sweets from somewhere he doesn't usually go, and the photo of Mochi printed! Yes, the photo is the real gift. He'll put it on the wall next to the calendar, I know him.
Also, my favourite izakaya in Tenma, "Kurumi", the master is also kind. Should I say goodbye there too? I feel silly, it's only 20 minutes by train, not another country.
You're right, I'll go one last time before the move, not as a goodbye but as "see you sometimes". No letter. Just eat and drink and say I'll come back.
And the new neighbourhood, Esaka, I don't know anything. How do I find "my places" in a new area?
Walk without a plan in the first weeks, go to the same café three times so they remember you, find the nearest bookshop and the best bakery. And check if there's a tofu shop! Okay, a mission.
Hello, quick update and then I work.
Still no answer from Ms. Fujimori, even after Grace's email. Grace says she'll call the agency next week, she has a Japanese-speaking colleague. So the novel is still waiting on the dialect answers.
And Kitsune: still undecided. I'll decide by the end of the month like I promised.

Game: 31,000 words done. Ahead of schedule. Elin sent the achievement icons, so now I can make the puns. One icon is a cat sleeping on a lantern. I named the achievement "Purr-manent Light". Too much?
Okay, you say puns are welcome per Elin's email and this one is visual and works with the icon. I keep it. Mochi approves (she is asleep).
Can you help me with one more: an achievement for lighting all the lanterns on the last island. Icon: a lighthouse at night with all windows lit. Japanese name 「すべての灯り」, "All the Lights".
"Every Light Burning" is beautiful but serious. "Lights, All of Them" is funny. "Keeper of Every Light" — oh, I like this, it connects to the title. Thank you.
Okay, back to work. Thank you for always being here, even at 6am.

HARBOR LANE PRESS LTD
14 Cloth Fair, London EC1A 7JQ, United Kingdom

TRANSLATION AGREEMENT (extract of principal terms)

Between: Harbor Lane Press Ltd ("the Publisher")
and: Yuki Tanabe, Osaka, Japan ("the Translator")

Work: SHIO NO KAJUEN by Kawabe Rin (original Japanese edition published by a Tokyo publisher), English title provisionally THE SALT ORCHARD ("the Work"). English-language translation rights licensed to the Publisher through Tsubaki Literary Agency, Tokyo.

1. COMMISSION. The Publisher commissions the Translator to translate the Work from Japanese into English, complete and without abridgement, in accordance with the Publisher's house style (British English spelling and punctuation).

2. DELIVERY.
2.1 The Translator shall deliver the translation of the first half of the Work (chapters 1 to 12 inclusive) by 15 November 2026.
2.2 The Translator shall deliver the complete translation by 31 January 2027.
2.3 The Translator shall respond to the editor's queries and review the copyedited text and proofs within the reasonable timescales set by the Publisher, normally not less than ten working days for each stage.

3. FEE.
3.1 The Publisher shall pay the Translator a fee of GBP 95 (ninety-five pounds sterling) per 1,000 words of the English translation as delivered and accepted. The length of the translation is estimated at 92,000 words, giving an estimated fee of GBP 8,740.
3.2 The fee shall be paid in three equal instalments based on the estimated fee: one third on signature of this Agreement by both parties; one third on delivery of the first half under clause 2.1; and the balance, adjusted to the final word count, on acceptance of the complete translation.

4. ROYALTY. Once the fee has been recouped, the Publisher shall pay the Translator a royalty of 1% of the Publisher's net receipts on all editions of the translation sold.

5. CREDIT. The Translator shall be credited by name on the front cover, the title page and in all publicity materials where the author is named.

6. QUERIES TO AUTHOR. Questions concerning the meaning of the original text shall be directed to the Author through the Author's agent, Tsubaki Literary Agency (contact: Ms. Fujimori Keiko). The Publisher will facilitate communication where necessary.

7. PUBLICATION. The Publisher intends to publish the translation within eighteen months of acceptance of the complete translation.

8. TAX. The Publisher will pay without deduction of UK tax upon receipt of a valid double taxation treaty form from the Translator.

9. MORAL RIGHTS. The Translator asserts the right to be identified as the translator of the Work.

10. COPYRIGHT. Copyright in the translation shall remain with the Translator, who grants the Publisher an exclusive licence for the full term of the Publisher's licence of the Work.

11. EDITING. The Publisher shall have the right to edit the translation for house style, clarity and length, but shall not make substantive changes to the meaning or tone without consulting the Translator. The Translator shall be sent the edited text, the copyedited text and one set of proofs for approval. Approval shall not be unreasonably withheld or delayed.

12. ACCEPTANCE. The Publisher shall notify the Translator within six (6) weeks of delivery of the complete translation whether it accepts the translation as satisfactory. If the Publisher reasonably considers the translation unsatisfactory, it shall specify in writing the changes required, and the Translator shall have a further six (6) weeks to make them.

13. TRANSLATOR'S NOTE. The Translator may contribute a translator's afterword of up to approximately 1,000 words, subject to the Publisher's editorial approval. No additional fee is payable for the afterword.

14. COPIES. The Translator shall receive ten (10) free copies of the first edition of the translation and may purchase further copies at a discount of 50% off the recommended retail price for personal use and not for resale.

15. SUBSIDIARY USE. Where the Publisher licenses the translation to third parties (for example, audio, serial or anthology rights), the Translator shall receive 10% of the Publisher's net receipts from such licences, in addition to the royalty under clause 4.

16. REVERSION. If the translation goes out of print and the Publisher does not reissue it within twelve (12) months of a written request by the Translator, the licence granted in clause 10 shall terminate and all rights in the translation shall revert to the Translator.

17. GOVERNING LAW. This Agreement shall be governed by the laws of England and Wales.

Editorial contact: Thomas Pryce, Senior Editor, thomas.pryce@harborlanepress.co.uk
Signed for the Publisher: ________________   Date: ________
Signed by the Translator: Yuki Tanabe        Date: 21 July 2026

documents.text:
PINECONE GAMES AB
Södermannagatan 19, 116 40 Stockholm, Sweden | org. nr. 559xxx-4471

STATEMENT OF WORK No. PG-LK-LOC-003
Under the Master Services Agreement dated 2 September 2026 between Pinecone Games AB ("Pinecone") and Yuki Tanabe ("Contractor")

Project: LANTERN KEEPER - Japanese to English localisation
Pinecone contact: Elin Berg, Producer (elin.berg@pineconegames.se)
Accounts: invoices@pineconegames.se

1. SCOPE
1.1 Translation and localisation of all in-game text for Lantern Keeper from Japanese into English (United States), including dialogue, UI, item descriptions, tutorial text, achievements and store page copy.
1.2 Estimated volume: 48,000 source-equivalent English words, as counted in the localisation spreadsheet provided by Pinecone (version 0.9).
1.3 Target locale: en-US. American spelling and punctuation conventions shall be used throughout (e.g., "color", "cozy"). The Pinecone style guide (v1.2) takes precedence where it differs.

2. RATE AND FEES
2.1 Rate: USD 0.11 per word of the estimated volume, i.e. an estimated fee of USD 5,280.
2.2 Changes in volume: if the final word count exceeds the estimate by more than 5%, the additional words shall be billed at the same per-word rate, upon written confirmation by Pinecone (a "Change Order"). Reductions in volume will reduce the fee accordingly.
2.3 Revisions: the fee includes up to three (3) rounds of revisions requested by Pinecone after the initial delivery. Additional revision rounds, and any rework caused by changes to source text after the string freeze, shall be billed at USD 45 per hour.

3. SCHEDULE
3.1 String freeze (no further source text changes without a Change Order): 20 November 2026.
3.2 First full delivery of localised text: 4 December 2026.
3.3 Final delivery after revisions and LQA (linguistic quality assurance) feedback: 18 December 2026.
3.4 Planned commercial release (for information only; not a Contractor obligation): 26 February 2027, Steam and Nintendo Switch.

4. MATERIALS
4.1 Pinecone will provide the localisation spreadsheet, the Pinecone style guide, a glossary of key terms, and, where available, reference screenshots and/or access to development builds under the confidentiality terms of the Master Services Agreement.

5. PAYMENT
5.1 The Contractor shall invoice 50% of the estimated fee on first full delivery and the remaining balance (adjusted for any Change Orders) on final delivery.
5.2 Invoices are payable within thirty (30) days of receipt, in USD by international bank transfer. Pinecone bears its own bank charges.

5.3 Change Orders: a Change Order may be requested by either party by email and becomes binding when confirmed in writing by the Pinecone producer. Each Change Order shall state the additional word count, the resulting fee adjustment and any change to the schedule.

5A. QUALITY ASSURANCE
5A.1 After first full delivery, Pinecone's LQA testers will review the localised text in the running build and log issues in the shared bug tracker. Issues will be categorised as Critical (meaning error, missing text, broken variable), Major (wrong tone, inconsistent terminology, text overflow) or Minor (style preference).
5A.2 The Contractor shall fix Critical and Major issues attributable to the translation within the revision rounds described in clause 2.3. Minor issues will be addressed at the Contractor's discretion where time allows.
5A.3 Issues caused by source text changes after the string freeze, missing context that Pinecone failed to provide, or engine limitations (for example, font or line-break problems) are not counted as revision rounds.

6. CREDIT
6.1 The Contractor will be credited in the game's end credits as "English Localization: Yuki Tanabe".

7. CONFIDENTIALITY
7.1 All materials, including story content, character names and builds, are confidential until the public release, in accordance with the Master Services Agreement.

Signed for Pinecone Games AB: Elin Berg, Producer, 30 September 2026
Signed by the Contractor: Yuki Tanabe, 1 October 2026

KAMOGAWA GARDEN HALL - WEDDING SCHEDULE NOTES (English version for family)
Couple: Aoi Tanabe & Daniel Weber
Date: Sunday, 18 April 2027
Planner: Hirano Mayumi (hirano@kamogawa-garden.jp, 075-555-0148). Please contact the planner, not the hall reception desk, for any questions.

THE DAY BEFORE - Saturday 17 April
- 15:00 Rehearsal in the Garden Chapel and the Garden Room (reception hall). Participants: couple, parents of both sides, Yuki Tanabe (sister of the bride, speech and family coordinator), MC, interpreter.
- 16:30 Final check of seating plan and gifts with the planner.

THE WEDDING DAY - Sunday 18 April
- 09:00 Family coordinators arrive (Yuki Tanabe for the bride's side; Mr. Jonas Weber, brother of the groom, for the groom's side).
- 09:30 Bride's hair, make-up and kimono dressing begins (bridal room, 2F).
- 11:30 Family photos in the garden (weather permitting; indoor alternative in the lobby).
- 12:30 Guests arrive; welcome drinks on the terrace.
- 13:00 Ceremony in the Garden Chapel (bilingual, Japanese and German/English, approx. 25 minutes).
- 13:45 Reception begins in the Garden Room (80 guests).
- 14:00 Welcome speech (groom's father), toast (bride's former teacher).
- 14:30 Meal service begins (French-Japanese course; see dietary notes).
- 15:15 Speech by the sister of the bride (Yuki Tanabe). Strictly maximum 3 minutes, including any translation, because of the timing of the kitchen service. Please send the final speech text to the planner by 31 March 2027 so that the MC and interpreter can prepare.
- 15:30 Bride's costume change (iro-uchikake to dress).
- 16:00 Cake cutting, games, video message from friends in Hamburg.
- 16:45 Letter from the bride to her parents; flower presentation.
- 17:15 Closing words (groom), guest send-off.
- 17:45 Family coordinators help guests from abroad with taxis to their hotels.

DIETARY NOTES
- Please inform the planner of all allergies by 15 March 2027.
- Already registered: Yuki Tanabe (buckwheat allergy - severe; kitchen will prepare a separate plate and avoid buckwheat in all shared items), Mrs. Weber (vegetarian).

DRESS CODE: Formal. Guests are kindly asked not to wear white. Kimono welcome.

PHOTOGRAPHY: Guests may take photos during the reception but not during the ceremony itself. The official photographer will share an online album within 6 weeks.

GIFTS: Return gifts (hikidemono) are arranged by the hall and will be placed at each seat. Monetary gifts may be handed in at the reception desk from 12:30.

She will interpret the welcome speech, the closing words and the letter from the bride. Family speeches that already include both languages (such as the speech by the sister of the bride) will not be interpreted again, but the interpreter will provide a short German summary card at each table of the groom's guests.

SEATING: The final seating plan must be confirmed by 1 April 2027. The head table will seat the couple only. Parents of both sides will be seated at the table nearest the entrance, according to Japanese custom. Guests from abroad will be seated together with at least one bilingual guest at each table where possible.

RAIN PLAN: If it rains, family photos will take place in the lobby and the welcome drinks will move from the terrace to the Garden Room foyer. The ceremony is indoors and will not be affected. The planner will decide the rain plan by 10:00 on the day.

ACCOMMODATION: A block of 12 rooms has been reserved at a partner hotel near Sanjo station for guests from abroad at a discounted rate, available until 18 March 2027. Please ask guests to book directly with the hotel quoting the reference "Tanabe-Weber".

TIMING REMINDER: The reception is scheduled to the minute because of the kitchen service. Speeches that run over will shorten the time for games and the video message. The MC has been asked to signal discreetly at 2 minutes 30 seconds.

TRANSPORT: The hall has no guest parking. The nearest station is Demachiyanagi (Keihan / Eizan line), 7 minutes on foot.

sleep question. i've been doing nights for years and i still sleep terribly on my days. 4 hours if i'm lucky. my friend sent this article, is any of it useful?

"Surviving the Night Shift: Evidence-Based Sleep Strategies for Shift Workers
Shift work disrupts the body's circadian rhythm, the internal clock that regulates sleep, alertness, hormone release and body temperature. Night workers are often trying to sleep at a time when their body is primed to be awake, which leads to shorter, lighter sleep.
Light management is one of the most powerful tools. Bright light exposure during the first half of the night shift can increase alertness. Conversely, avoiding bright light on the commute home - by wearing sunglasses, for example - can help the body prepare for sleep. The bedroom should be completely dark, using blackout blinds or an eye mask.
Anchor sleep: some research suggests that keeping a consistent 'anchor' period of sleep (for example, from 9am to 1pm) on both work days and days off can help stabilise the circadian rhythm.
Pre-shift nap: a nap of 60-90 minutes before a night shift can reduce sleepiness during the shift. Short naps of 20 minutes during breaks can also help, if permitted.
Caffeine: caffeine can improve alertness, but should be avoided in the last 4-6 hours before planned sleep. Many night workers drink coffee late in their shift, which then impairs daytime sleep.
Food: large, heavy meals during the night can cause indigestion and drowsiness. Smaller meals and snacks are recommended, with a light meal before daytime sleep.
Noise: use earplugs or white noise, inform household members of sleep times, and put the phone on 'do not disturb'.
Transitioning back: after a run of nights, a short sleep in the morning (2-3 hours) followed by staying awake until a normal bedtime can help reset to a day schedule.
Long-term health: chronic shift work is associated with increased risk of cardiovascular disease, metabolic problems and mood disorders. Regular health checks, physical activity and social support are important."

lit review help. here's a paragraph from my dissertation lit review, dr patel says it's "descriptive rather than critical". what does he mean, and how do i fix it?

"Many studies have examined the reasons why newly qualified nurses leave their jobs. Smith et al. (2019) conducted a survey of 450 newly qualified nurses in England and found that 38% were considering leaving within the first year, with the main reasons being workload, lack of support and poor staffing. Jones and Ahmed (2021) carried out interviews with 22 nurses and found that a lack of preceptorship and feeling unable to speak up were important factors. Brown (2020) found that newly qualified nurses who had a structured preceptorship programme were more likely to stay. Williams et al. (2022) conducted a systematic review of 31 studies and found that the most common factors associated with leaving were workload, ward culture, and the gap between expectations and reality, sometimes called 'reality shock'. Patel and O'Connor (2023) found that pay was a less important factor than expected in their study of 300 nurses in Scotland, but this was before the cost of living crisis. ok so it's a list: "X found this, Y found that". critical means comparing and evaluating: where do studies agree, where do they disagree, what are the strengths and weaknesses of the methods, and what's missing. like "Smith's large survey shows the scale but can't explain why; Jones and Ahmed's interviews add depth but with 22 participants from one trust...". and the Patel and O'Connor point about pay before the cost of living crisis is actually a gap i can use!
can you rewrite it in a critical way as an example? i'll then write mine in my own words, i'm not copying, promise

dissertation background reading. dr patel wants me to put my study in the "policy context". here's a summary article i found about NHS workforce policy, can you help me pull out what's relevant to newly qualified nurse retention?

"NHS Workforce Policy and the Retention Challenge: An Overview
Over the past decade, NHS workforce policy in England has increasingly shifted its emphasis from recruitment towards retention. While international recruitment and expanded training places have increased the number of nurses joining the register, the number leaving the profession or the NHS remains a significant concern. Analysis of NMC and NHS data suggests that leaver rates are highest among nurses in the early years of their careers and among those approaching retirement.
Several national initiatives have targeted retention. The NHS People Plan placed emphasis on flexible working, health and wellbeing support, and creating a more inclusive culture. A national preceptorship framework was introduced to standardise support for newly registered nurses, setting out minimum expectations for protected learning time, a named preceptor, and structured reviews during the first 12 months. Trusts have been encouraged to appoint preceptorship leads and to monitor completion rates.
Long-term workforce planning documents have set ambitious targets to reduce leaver rates, alongside expanding apprenticeships and alternative routes into nursing. Critics have argued that targets are not matched by investment in the conditions that drive retention, such as safe staffing levels, pay, and the physical working environment, including access to rest areas and hot food on night shifts.
The cost-of-living crisis has added new pressures. Surveys by professional bodies have reported that significant proportions of nurses are struggling financially, with some taking second jobs or bank shifts to make ends meet, which may increase burnout. Industrial action in 2022-2023 highlighted dissatisfaction with pay and conditions.
Research on retention identifies a combination of 'push' factors (workload, staffing, incivility, lack of support, moral distress) and 'pull' factors (career development opportunities, flexible working, supportive leadership, team belonging). For newly qualified nurses specifically, the transition from student to registrant - often described as 'transition shock' or 'reality shock' - is a critical period, and the quality of preceptorship and ward culture during this period appears to be particularly influential.
Local leadership is repeatedly highlighted as a key lever. Ward managers and ward sisters shape the day-to-day experience of staff, including allocation of work, access to development, and whether staff feel able to raise concerns. However, these leaders often report having little protected time for staff support, as they are drawn into operational pressures."

ok, so for my policy context: the shift from recruitment to retention, the national preceptorship framework (that's directly relevant, my survey asks about preceptors!), the push/pull factors framing, the cost of living stuff, and local leadership as a lever. that last bit is basically "ward sisters matter" which i will absolutely be quoting lol
the "access to rest areas and hot food on night shifts" made me laugh-cry. we have a vending machine and a microwave that's been broken since june
can you suggest a structure for the policy context section? about 800 words

good: national picture (numbers), policy response (people plan, preceptorship framework), critiques (investment gap, cost of living), and then "the local leadership gap" leading into my research question. that flows nicely into "why do they stay"
and push/pull factors, is that a proper theoretical framework i can cite, or just a description?

ok, it comes from migration theory originally and has been applied to workforce studies, so it's citable but i should present it as a lens, not a full theory. and maybe pair it with something like job embeddedness theory for the "stay" side. ooh. dr patel will like that
what is job embeddedness in one paragraph?

"links, fit and sacrifice": how connected you are to people at work, how well the job fits you, and what you'd give up by leaving. that's literally what my open questions are getting at. ok i'm actually excited about this now
night x

complaint response help. Bev asked me to draft the response to a complaint as practice for when i'm acting manager. it's anonymised. here's the complaint:

"I am writing to complain about the care my father received on Ward 12 during his admission last month. My father is 82 and has COPD and mild dementia. On the evening he was admitted, he was left in a chair for over four hours because there was no bed available on the ward, and nobody explained to us why. When he was eventually moved to a bed, his hearing aids were left behind in the assessment unit and it took two days for them to be found, during which time he became very confused and distressed because he could not hear what was being said to him. On the second night, he was found on the floor next to his bed at 3am. We were not informed until the next morning when we visited, and we only found out because my father told us. The nurse we spoke to was very kind but said she was not on duty that night. I understand the NHS is under pressure, but I feel my father's basic needs were not met and that we as a family were not kept informed. I would like to know what happened on the night of the fall, why we were not told, and what will be done to make sure this does not happen to other patients."

oof. ok so the facts from our side: no bed due to the ward being full, he was in the chair in the assessment unit not on our ward actually, hearing aids lost in transfer, the fall was reported on datix and he had no injuries, but the family should have been called that night or at least first thing in the morning by the nurse in charge and it didn't happen. that's on us

here's my draft response, it's too defensive, i can feel it:

"Dear Mrs X,
Thank you for your letter regarding your father's recent admission to Ward 12. I am sorry that you were unhappy with aspects of his care.
I would like to explain that on the evening of your father's admission, the hospital was experiencing extremely high demand and there were no beds available on Ward 12. Your father was cared for in the Acute Assessment Unit until a bed became available. This was outside the control of the ward staff.
Regarding your father's hearing aids, these were unfortunately mislaid during his transfer between departments. The hearing aids were located two days later.
On the night of [date], your father was found on the floor next to his bed. Staff assessed him immediately and he was found to have no injuries. A full review was carried out, and an incident report was completed in line with trust policy. Unfortunately, the family were not contacted at the time.
We take all complaints seriously and your feedback will be shared with the ward team.
Yours sincerely,
Ward Sister, Ward 12"

yes. "i am sorry that you were unhappy" is the classic non-apology. and "outside the control of the ward staff" sounds like passing the blame. and "unfortunately the family were not contacted" is passive, it hides that we got it wrong

can you rewrite it so it's a genuine apology, explains what happened, owns the bits we got wrong, and says specifically what we're changing? the changes are: hearing aids and glasses go in a labelled bag that travels WITH the patient and is checked at handover, and the nurse in charge must contact the family after any fall within the shift (or document why not), and we're adding it to the night handover checklist

oh that's so much better. "I am sorry that your father was distressed and that you were not told about his fall. You should have been informed that night, and I apologise that this did not happen." clear and honest. and the duty of candour bit, saying we'd like to meet them to talk it through. yes
should i offer a meeting in person? bev says it often helps
yes, offer it, with me and maybe Femi, and let them choose phone or face to face. people mostly just want to be heard. ok
i'll send this to Bev tomorrow. thank you. this is the side of the manager job that scares me more than the rota

"Staff Seasonal Influenza Vaccination Programme - Frequently Asked Questions
Why should I have the flu vaccine? Influenza is a serious illness that can lead to hospitalisation and death, particularly in older people, those with long-term conditions and pregnant women. Healthcare workers are at increased risk of exposure to influenza and can transmit the virus to vulnerable patients, colleagues and family members, even if they have mild or no symptoms. Vaccination of healthcare workers reduces the risk of transmission and helps maintain safe staffing levels during the winter period.
Can the vaccine give me flu? No. The injectable flu vaccines used in adults do not contain live virus and cannot cause influenza. Some people experience mild side effects such as a sore arm, mild fever or aching muscles for a day or two, which is a sign that the immune system is responding.
I had the vaccine last year. Do I need it again? Yes. Flu viruses change each year and the vaccine is updated to match the strains expected to circulate. Protection from the vaccine also wanes over time.
I am pregnant. Is it safe? Yes. The flu vaccine is recommended for pregnant women at any stage of pregnancy and also provides some protection to the baby in the first months of life.
I have an egg allergy. Can I have it? Most people with egg allergy can safely receive the vaccine. Please discuss with the occupational health team if you have had a severe reaction in the past.
Where can I get it? Peer vaccinators are available on most wards, and drop-in clinics are held in the staff restaurant on weekdays from 11:00 to 14:00 throughout October and November. Night staff can request a visit from a peer vaccinator during their shift."

tobi is a sheep in the nativity and he is taking it VERY seriously. he asked me to write him a story about "the sheep who saw baby jesus". so i did, at 4am on my break. is it ok for a 4 year old? be honest:

"Once upon a time, on a cold, starry night, there was a little sheep called Tobi. Tobi was the smallest sheep on the hill, and the other sheep always said, 'You're too small to see anything, Tobi!'
That night, the sky was very dark and very quiet. All the sheep were sleeping, and the shepherds were sitting by the fire, yawning.
Suddenly, the sky was full of light! Bright, golden light, brighter than a hundred torches. The shepherds jumped up. The sheep woke up. 'Baaa!' they said. 'What is it?'
An angel appeared, shining and kind. 'Don't be afraid,' said the angel. 'A special baby has been born in Bethlehem. Go and see!'
The shepherds started walking down the hill, and all the big sheep followed. But Tobi was so small that he got left behind. 'Wait for me!' he called. But nobody heard.
Tobi walked and walked. His little legs were tired. Then he looked up, and he saw a big, bright star in the sky. 'I'll follow the star,' said Tobi.
The star led Tobi all the way to a little stable. Inside, there was a mummy, a daddy, and a tiny baby sleeping in a manger full of hay. The big sheep were all standing at the back, but they were so big they couldn't see over the shepherds.
But Tobi was small. He walked right between the shepherds' legs, all the way to the front, and he saw the baby. The baby opened his eyes and looked at Tobi and smiled.
'See,' said the mummy softly, 'sometimes the smallest ones see the most.'
And Tobi the sheep curled up next to the manger, warm and happy, and went to sleep.
The End."

documents.text:
PENNINE UNIVERSITY
Faculty of Health and Social Care - Research Ethics Committee

To: Oluwaseun Adeyemi, MSc Healthcare Leadership (part-time), Student ID on file
Supervisor: Dr Helen Marsh
Date: 19 August 2026
Reference: FHSC-REC-2026-0388

Study title: "Why do they stay? A mixed-methods study of retention among newly qualified nurses in an NHS acute trust"

Dear Oluwaseun,

I am pleased to inform you that the Faculty Research Ethics Committee has reviewed your application and has granted a FAVOURABLE OPINION, subject to the following conditions:

1. Approval period: This approval is valid until 31 August 2027. If data collection or analysis is not completed by this date, you must apply for an extension.

2. Participants: Registered nurses employed by the host trust who qualified (first NMC registration) no more than 24 months before the date of participation. The maximum sample is 120 participants for the survey and 12 participants for the interviews.

3. Conflict of interest: Because of the researcher's role as a ward sister, the Committee requires that NO participants be recruited from the researcher's own ward or from any staff the researcher line-manages or supervises. Recruitment must be through a neutral channel (e.g. the practice education team mailing list), and invitations must not be sent by the researcher personally to individual colleagues.

4. Consent: Survey participants must confirm consent electronically before accessing the questionnaire. Interview participants must sign the approved consent form (version 2, dated 12 August 2026) and must be given at least 48 hours between receiving the information sheet and the interview.

5. Data management: All data must be stored on the university's secure OneDrive account only. Data must not be stored on personal devices, personal cloud accounts or NHS shared drives. Interview recordings must be deleted after transcription and anonymisation, and no later than 3 months after the interview.

6. NHS permissions: This favourable opinion does not constitute permission to conduct research in the NHS. You must obtain confirmation of capacity and capability from the host trust's Research and Development (R&D) department before any recruitment begins.

7. Amendments: Any changes to the study design, recruitment strategy, participant materials or data management must be submitted to the Committee as an amendment and approved before implementation.

8. Reporting: A brief end-of-study report must be submitted within 3 months of completion.

9. Withdrawal: Survey participants may withdraw by closing the browser before submitting; once submitted, anonymous survey responses cannot be withdrawn, and this must be stated in the information sheet. Interview participants may withdraw up to 2 weeks after their interview, after which data will have been anonymised and incorporated into the analysis.

10. Participant support: The information sheet must include signposting to the trust's staff wellbeing service and the Freedom to Speak Up Guardian, given that participants may discuss distressing experiences. If a participant discloses a serious patient safety concern or risk of harm, the researcher must follow the trust's escalation procedures and should discuss this with the supervisor.

11. Monitoring: The Committee may audit approved studies at any time. You must retain the signed consent forms and a copy of all participant materials for the duration of the approval and for 5 years thereafter, in line with university policy.

Please keep this letter for your records and include a copy in your dissertation appendices.

Yours sincerely,
Professor Anne Whitaker
Chair, Faculty Research Ethics Committee

E-TICKET ITINERARY / RECEIPT
Equator Airways & partner carrier
Booking reference: K7QXRM
Passenger: MRS FOLAKE ADEYEMI
Ticket number: 389-2241186027
Frequent flyer: none

OUTBOUND - Lagos to Manchester
Flight 1: EQ 0571 - Lagos (LOS) Murtala Muhammed Intl, Terminal 2 -> Amsterdam (AMS) Schiphol
Departure: Friday 13 November 2026, 22:35 (local time)
Arrival: Saturday 14 November 2026, 05:25 (local time)
Cabin: Economy (class Q) | Seat: 31C (aisle, requested)

Connection in Amsterdam: 2 h 10 min

Flight 2: EQ 1187 operated by partner carrier - Amsterdam (AMS) -> Manchester (MAN), Terminal 2
Departure: Saturday 14 November 2026, 07:35
Arrival: Saturday 14 November 2026, 07:55 (local time)
Cabin: Economy | Seat: 14D

RETURN - Manchester to Lagos
Flight 3: EQ 1190 operated by partner carrier - Manchester (MAN) Terminal 2 -> Amsterdam (AMS)
Departure: Saturday 13 February 2027, 10:40
Arrival: Saturday 13 February 2027, 13:00

Flight 4: EQ 0572 - Amsterdam (AMS) -> Lagos (LOS) Terminal 2
Departure: Saturday 13 February 2027, 15:20
Arrival: Saturday 13 February 2027, 21:05 (local time)

BAGGAGE ALLOWANCE (per passenger, all flights):
- Checked baggage: 2 pieces, max 23 kg each
- Cabin baggage: 1 piece, max 12 kg, plus 1 personal item (handbag)
Excess baggage must be paid at the airport and is charged per piece.

SPECIAL SERVICES:
- Passenger assistance (wheelchair to/from aircraft) can be requested up to 48 hours before departure by contacting the airline.
- Special meals: none requested. Can be requested up to 24 hours before departure.

FARE CONDITIONS:
- Date changes permitted with a fee of USD 150 plus any fare difference.
- Refund: non-refundable, except taxes.
- No-show on any segment cancels the remaining segments.

Travel documents: Passenger is responsible for holding a valid passport and UK Standard Visitor visa. Please arrive at the airport at least 3 hours before international departures.

IMPORTANT INFORMATION:
- Online check-in opens 30 hours before departure and closes 90 minutes before departure. Boarding passes for the connecting flight will be issued at the first check-in.
- Transit in Amsterdam: passengers remain airside; no Schengen visa is required for a direct airside transfer. Follow the signs for Transfers. Allow time for security screening at the transfer point.
- Liquids in cabin baggage: maximum 100 ml per container in a single transparent bag.
- Restricted items: meat, milk and dairy products may not be brought into the UK from outside the EU for personal use. Other food items may be subject to restrictions; passengers are advised to declare any food items on arrival if unsure.
- Medication: carry prescription medication in the original packaging in cabin baggage, with a copy of the prescription or a doctor's letter.
- Delays: in case of a missed connection due to a delay of the first flight, the airline will rebook the passenger on the next available flight at no extra cost.
